meta.blurb: Margaret Hale grew up among green fields, and the smoky mill town of Milton feels like another world. John Thornton, its proudest owner, thinks she looks down on him, and he may be right. Then a strike begins.
meta.bible: Margaret Hale: the heroine, eighteen at the start, honest, brave and a little proud; she grew up in the south. Mr Hale: her father, a gentle clergyman who leaves the church over matters of conscience and becomes a private tutor. Mrs Hale: her mother, delicate and sad to leave the south; she dies in Milton. Frederick Hale: Margaret's brother, a sailor who took part in a mutiny against a cruel captain and lives in exile abroad. John Thornton: a Milton cotton mill owner, strong, serious and proud; he rose from poverty. Hannah Thornton: his strict, devoted mother. Fanny Thornton: his younger sister. Nicholas Higgins: a mill worker and union man, honest and stubborn. Bessy Higgins: his daughter, who is dying of lung disease from cotton dust. Boucher: a striker whose death leaves his children alone. Mr Bell: Mr Hale's old friend from Oxford, Margaret's godfather and landlord of Marlborough Mills; he dies and leaves Margaret his fortune. Mrs Shaw: Margaret's aunt, who lives in London. Edith Lennox: Margaret's cousin, who marries Captain Lennox. Captain Lennox: Edith's husband. Henry Lennox: the captain's brother, a lawyer; he proposes to Margaret and is refused. Dixon: the Hales' faithful servant. Leonards: the man who tries to arrest Frederick at the station and falls. Helstone: the quiet southern village where the Hales live at first. Milton: the northern mill town, based on Manchester, full of smoke and noise. Marlborough Mills: Thornton's cotton mill. Harley Street: Mrs Shaw's London house. Oxford: where Mr Hale dies. Spain: where Frederick lives. England. Author: Elizabeth Gaskell, published 1854 to 1855. Voice and tone: serious, warm and social-minded; a love story set against a strike; deaths are stated plainly, with no gore; the ending is hopeful. Added for the full-length book: Aunt Shaw and Mrs Shaw are the same person, the widow in Harley Street. Hampshire: the county of Helstone and its great forest. Corfu: the island where Captain Lennox's regiment is posted. Crampton: the Milton suburb where the Hales rent a plain house. Dr Donaldson: the Milton doctor who attends Mrs Hale. Mr Hamper: a rich mill owner who talks of masters and hands. Mr Slickson: a mill owner at the Thorntons' dinner. The police inspector: questions Margaret about the station. Hands: what masters call their workers. Union: the workers' club that calls the strike. Orion: Frederick's ship, where the mutiny took place. Iliad: the poem by Homer that Mr Hale and Mr Thornton read together. Irish: the labourers brought in to break the strike. Balliol and Oxford: Mr Bell's old college and town. Bible, Church, Sunday, Christmas, Latin, Greek, English, French, Spanish: things named in passing. Voice: warm, serious, with long, clear sentences at the higher levels.

beats.scene: Margaret in a London drawing room helps her cousin Edith dress for a wedding
beats.summary: On the day before the wedding, Margaret helps her cousin Edith try on her gown in Mrs Shaw's London house.

beats.scene: Edith lies on a sofa chatting happily while Margaret holds a mirror
beats.summary: Edith, spoiled and happy, talks of Captain Lennox and the island of Corfu where his regiment will be posted.

beats.scene: A grand London house with servants hurrying through rooms full of flowers
beats.summary: Margaret has lived in her aunt's house since childhood and feels more like a guest than a daughter.

beats.scene: A young lawyer with clever eyes enters the drawing room carrying a book
beats.summary: Henry Lennox, the Captain's younger brother and a lawyer, calls at Harley Street.

beats.scene: Margaret and Henry laugh together by a tall window overlooking a London square

beats.scene: Edith stands in white at the church door beside Captain Lennox

beats.scene: Wedding guests raise glasses at a long table under a chandelier
beats.summary: At the wedding breakfast Henry Lennox tells Margaret he hopes to visit her in Hampshire.

beats.scene: A carriage with white ribbons drives away as Mrs Shaw waves a handkerchief
beats.summary: The bride and groom leave, and the great house falls silent.

beats.scene: Margaret alone in a tidy bedroom packs a small trunk by lamplight
beats.summary: Margaret sorts her belongings and thinks about her years in London and her longing for home.

beats.scene: A railway carriage window shows green fields and hedges rushing past
beats.summary: Margaret takes the train south to Helstone and her parents.

beats.scene: Margaret steps from a carriage at a small vicarage covered in roses
beats.summary: Margaret reaches Helstone and is welcomed by her father, her mother and the servant Dixon.

beats.scene: A clergyman and his daughter walk along a forest lane to a cottage
beats.summary: Margaret walks with her father through the village and visits the cottagers, who greet her warmly.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale rests on a sofa in a sunny parlour as Margaret sews
beats.summary: Margaret's mother, delicate and often tired, tells her she misses the grander life of her youth.

beats.scene: Henry Lennox in a travelling coat arrives at the vicarage gate
beats.summary: Henry Lennox comes to Helstone and Mr Hale welcomes him as a guest.

beats.scene: Two men talk over open books in a small study lined with shelves
beats.summary: Henry and Mr Hale discuss books, and Margaret shows Henry her favourite places.

beats.scene: Margaret and Henry walk side by side beneath tall trees in the forest
beats.summary: On a long walk, Margaret begins to sense that Henry hopes for more than friendship.

beats.scene: Henry speaks earnestly to Margaret among the roses of the vicarage garden
beats.summary: In the garden Henry tells Margaret that he loves her and asks her to marry him.

beats.scene: Margaret shakes her head gently while Henry looks down at the gravel
beats.summary: Margaret refuses him kindly but plainly, and Henry is deeply hurt.

beats.scene: Henry bows stiffly at the gate and walks away along the road
beats.summary: Henry leaves Helstone, saying he does not mean to give up hope.

beats.scene: Margaret sits alone on a garden bench as the evening light fades
beats.summary: Margaret is relieved and puzzled, and she notices that her father looks troubled.

beats.scene: Mr Hale sits pale and silent at a supper table lit by candles
beats.summary: At supper Mr Hale is restless and silent, and Margaret fears that something is wrong.

beats.scene: A clergyman and his daughter walk slowly along a shaded village lane
beats.summary: On a walk, Mr Hale tells Margaret that he has doubts and must leave the Church.

beats.scene: Mr Hale explains himself to Margaret with a worn prayer book in his hands
beats.summary: He explains that he cannot honestly continue as a clergyman, and that his mind is made up.

beats.scene: Margaret listens at the garden gate as her father speaks of leaving home
beats.summary: Margaret understands what the decision will cost: the home, the income and the quiet life.

beats.scene: Margaret sits beside her mother on a sofa and speaks in a low voice
beats.summary: Mr Hale cannot bring himself to tell his wife, so Margaret does it for him.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale weeps into a handkerchief while Dixon stands angrily in the doorway
beats.summary: Mrs Hale is stunned and tearful, and the faithful servant Dixon is furious.

beats.scene: Mr Hale writes a letter at his desk by lamplight
beats.summary: Mr Hale writes to the bishop to resign, and then to his old friend Mr Bell for advice.

beats.scene: An old letter lies open on a table beside a map of northern England
beats.summary: Mr Bell answers that Mr Hale could earn a living as a tutor in Milton, a manufacturing town.

beats.scene: Margaret reads aloud a description of a smoky northern town to her parents
beats.summary: The family hears about Milton, a busy and crowded place, and Margaret tries to hide her dismay.

beats.scene: Margaret and her father stand together in the parlour, packing cases beside them
beats.summary: Mr Hale decides to go, and the family begins to plan the move.

beats.scene: Margaret says goodbye to an old oak tree and a cottage garden
beats.summary: In her last days at Helstone, Margaret visits her favourite places and says goodbye to the cottagers.

beats.scene: Villagers fill a small stone church as Mr Hale speaks his last sermon
beats.summary: On the final Sunday the villagers weep as Mr Hale says farewell to them.

beats.scene: Dixon packs china and books into wooden crates in a cluttered hall
beats.summary: The house is emptied, and Mrs Hale is too unwell to travel, so Margaret and her father go ahead.

beats.scene: A train carries a father and daughter north past fading green hills
beats.summary: Margaret and Mr Hale travel north, and she watches the countryside change.

beats.scene: A grey cloud of smoke hangs over a distant town with tall chimneys

beats.scene: Crowds of workers in clogs and shawls hurry through a noisy street
beats.summary: In the streets Margaret sees women in shawls and hears a strange, blunt way of speaking.

beats.scene: A house agent shows an unhappy family a row of ugly brick houses
beats.summary: The house agent shows them houses that are too grand or too dismal, and money is short.

beats.scene: Margaret stands in the doorway of a plain brick house with small windows
beats.summary: They choose a modest rented house in Crampton, and Margaret does her best to like it.

beats.scene: Margaret hangs curtains and arranges books in a small, dingy parlour
beats.summary: Margaret works hard to make the rooms homelike before her mother comes.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale sits pale in a hired carriage as chimneys rise outside the window
beats.summary: Mrs Hale and Dixon arrive, and the first night in Milton is full of strange noises.

beats.scene: Dixon scrubs a grey film of soot from a parlour windowsill
beats.summary: Soot settles on everything in the house, and Dixon complains about the north.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale lies in bed describing the roses of Helstone to Margaret
beats.summary: Mrs Hale is low in spirits and talks constantly of the life she has left behind.

beats.scene: Mr Hale in his small study spreads out books for his first lessons
beats.summary: Mr Hale is cheerful about his plans as a private tutor, and he finds the town interesting.

beats.scene: Margaret walks past warehouses and a canal in a busy street of carts
beats.summary: Margaret explores the town and is struck by its noise, its wagons and its energy.

beats.scene: A mill bell rings and hundreds of workers pour out into the street
beats.summary: A mill bell rings at midday, and the workers stream out, talking and laughing.

beats.scene: A mill girl reaches out to touch the shawl on Margaret's shoulders
beats.summary: A group of mill girls speaks to Margaret with friendly boldness, and she answers them kindly.

beats.scene: Margaret tells her father about the workers over a plain evening meal
beats.summary: Margaret learns that the workers are called hands, and Mr Hale mentions Mr Bell's tenant, Mr Thornton.

beats.scene: Dixon returns from the market with a basket and a long list of complaints
beats.summary: Dixon struggles with the market, the prices and the northern manners, but she is loyal.

beats.scene: Margaret works at a table covered with household accounts and receipts
beats.summary: Margaret takes charge of the household and learns how carefully money must be spent.

beats.scene: Margaret lies awake at her window as the mill lamps glow through the dark
beats.summary: Mr Hale announces that his first pupil will be Mr Thornton, and Margaret wonders what he is like.

beats.scene: A tall dark man in a plain coat bows stiffly in a small parlour
beats.summary: Mr Thornton arrives for his first lesson, and he and Margaret form a poor first impression of each other.

beats.scene: Mr Thornton and Mr Hale sit over an open book of Greek poetry
beats.summary: Mr Thornton asks to study the classics, and the two men begin to read Homer's Iliad together.

beats.scene: Margaret frowns at a tray of tea as Mr Thornton speaks about trade
beats.summary: Margaret says something scornful about trade, and Mr Thornton answers with quiet pride.

beats.scene: Mr Hale smiles warmly as he talks with his pupil in the lamplit study
beats.summary: Mr Hale grows fond of Mr Thornton, and Margaret listens to their talk from the next room.

beats.scene: A stern grey-haired woman sits stiffly on a chair in the Hales' parlour
beats.summary: Mrs Thornton calls at Crampton, polite and cold, and studies Margaret closely.

beats.scene: A huge mill with rows of lit windows stands beside a stone house
beats.summary: The Hales return the visit at Marlborough Mills, and Margaret sees the great mill for the first time.

beats.scene: Mrs Thornton sits in a stiff parlour filled with covered furniture
beats.summary: In Mrs Thornton's formal parlour Margaret finds a woman who guards her son as her proudest work.

beats.scene: A pretty girl in a fashionable dress asks Margaret about London fashions
beats.summary: Fanny Thornton, the daughter, chatters about fashions and seems to admire Margaret's London manners.

beats.scene: Mr Thornton crosses a busy mill yard as the workers touch their caps
beats.summary: Margaret watches Mr Thornton among his men and sees that they respect and fear him.

beats.scene: Margaret frowns on the walk home while her father speaks warmly of Mr Thornton
beats.summary: Margaret decides she does not like Mr Thornton, but her father defends him warmly.

beats.scene: A thin young woman coughs at a street corner as Margaret passes
beats.summary: On a walk Margaret meets Bessy Higgins, a pale mill girl, and her sister Mary.

beats.scene: Bessy sits on a doorstep holding her chest and looking at the sky
beats.summary: Bessy explains that the cotton fluff in the mill air has made her ill and that she expects to die.

beats.scene: Margaret steps into a small, neat kitchen with a scrubbed table and a fire
beats.summary: Margaret visits the Higgins family home and finds it poor but clean.

beats.scene: A broad-shouldered workman sits by the fire and speaks bluntly to Margaret
beats.summary: Nicholas Higgins comes home and speaks plainly about how the masters treat the workers.

beats.scene: Margaret and Higgins face each other across the kitchen table
beats.summary: Higgins is wary of ladies, but Margaret answers him directly, and he begins to respect her.

beats.scene: Margaret reads aloud to Bessy from a worn Bible by a window
beats.summary: Bessy loves the last book of the Bible, for its promise of a place without pain.

beats.scene: Mr Hale talks gently with Higgins by the fire in the kitchen
beats.summary: Mr Hale visits the Higgins family, and the two men talk about faith and doubt.

beats.scene: Men in caps whisper together on a street corner at dusk
beats.summary: Higgins speaks of the Union and says the workers may soon stop work to demand fair pay.

beats.scene: Margaret sits at her mother's bedside as Dixon grumbles at the door
beats.summary: Mrs Hale grows weaker, and Dixon disapproves of Margaret's visits to mill families.

beats.scene: Margaret stands at a window at dusk looking over the rooftops of Milton
beats.summary: Margaret sees that the masters and the workers live in two different worlds, and she wants to understand both.

beats.scene: Mr Thornton talks by the fire with Margaret and her father
beats.summary: Mr Thornton tells the Hales how he rose from poverty when his father died and left the family in debt.

beats.scene: Margaret listens in silence with her sewing lying forgotten in her lap
beats.summary: Margaret is moved by his story, though she does not say so.

beats.scene: Margaret fastens a plain dress in front of a small mirror
beats.summary: The Hales are invited to dinner at Marlborough Mills, and Margaret goes with her father.

beats.scene: A grand dining table gleams with silver and glass in the Thorntons' house
beats.summary: At the dinner, the mill owners and their wives eat a very rich meal.

beats.scene: Mill owners in dark coats lean over their wine and talk loudly
beats.summary: Mr Hamper and other masters say that the workers should simply obey.

beats.scene: Mr Slickson laughs while Margaret sits quietly and listens
beats.summary: The masters speak of the hands as if they were children, and Margaret grows indignant.

beats.scene: Margaret speaks earnestly to Mr Thornton in a quiet corner of the drawing room
beats.summary: After dinner Margaret tells Mr Thornton that she thinks he is too hard on his workers.

beats.scene: Mr Thornton answers with a clenched hand resting on a mantelpiece
beats.summary: Mr Thornton answers that a master must be free to run his own mill as he sees fit.

beats.scene: Mrs Thornton and Fanny watch the couple from across the room
beats.summary: The argument ends coldly, and Mrs Thornton and Fanny notice the tension between them.

beats.scene: Mr Thornton walks alone in his study at night, thinking
beats.summary: Margaret goes home regretting her sharp words, and Mr Thornton cannot forget her.

beats.scene: Margaret reads a worn letter by candlelight in her bedroom
beats.summary: Margaret keeps a family secret: her brother Frederick, a sailor, lives in exile abroad.

beats.scene: A young sailor in a dark coat stands on a ship's deck at night
beats.summary: Margaret remembers why Frederick cannot come home: he took part in a mutiny against a cruel captain.

beats.scene: A kind doctor listens at Mrs Hale's chest while Margaret waits anxiously
beats.summary: Dr Donaldson finds Mrs Hale very ill, and Margaret fears for her mother.

beats.scene: Mill owners sit around a table with papers and agree on lower wages
beats.summary: In a hard season for trade, the masters agree to hold wages down.

beats.scene: Higgins stands in the Hales' parlour with his cap in his hands
beats.summary: Higgins tells Margaret the men will turn out if the masters will not listen.

beats.scene: Workers stand with their tools down outside a closed mill gate
beats.summary: The workers stop work together, and the mills fall silent.

beats.scene: A thin man named Boucher stands in a doorway with hungry children
beats.summary: In the poor streets food runs short, and Boucher's family is hungriest of all.

beats.scene: Mr Thornton stands firm at his office desk reading a letter
beats.summary: Mr Thornton refuses to bend and decides to bring in workers from Ireland.

beats.scene: Margaret speaks urgently to Mr Thornton in the Hales' parlour
beats.summary: Margaret begs Mr Thornton not to bring in new workers, but he says it is the only way.

beats.scene: Boucher shouts to a group of angry men beside a dark canal
beats.summary: Boucher stirs up the strikers, and Higgins fears that trouble is coming.

beats.scene: Irish labourers step from a train and walk through a silent crowd
beats.summary: The Irish workers arrive at the mill under guard, and the strikers watch them in fury.

beats.scene: An angry crowd presses against the iron gates of a great mill
beats.summary: The crowd grows, and Higgins tries in vain to calm the men.

beats.scene: Margaret hurries through crowded streets with a covered basket
beats.summary: Margaret goes to Marlborough Mills with a message and finds the house surrounded.

beats.scene: Stones strike the windows of the Thorntons' house as the family hides
beats.summary: The mob throws stones at the windows, and troops are sent for.

beats.scene: Margaret speaks urgently to Mr Thornton at a window above the crowd
beats.summary: Margaret begs Mr Thornton to speak to the mob before the soldiers shoot.

beats.scene: Mr Thornton walks out of the door into a roaring crowd of workers
beats.summary: Mr Thornton steps outside alone, and Margaret follows him.

beats.scene: Margaret throws her arms around Mr Thornton as a stone flies
beats.summary: Margaret shields Mr Thornton with her body, and a stone strikes her forehead.

beats.scene: Mr Thornton lifts Margaret as the crowd falls suddenly silent
beats.summary: The crowd sees a woman hurt and begins to back away in shame.

beats.scene: Soldiers in red coats march into the empty mill yard
beats.summary: Soldiers arrive and the mob scatters, leaving the yard quiet.

beats.scene: Mrs Thornton and Fanny kneel beside Margaret in the parlour
beats.summary: Margaret is taken inside and cared for, and Mrs Thornton is cold and wary.

beats.scene: Margaret rests on a sofa with a bandaged forehead as her father watches
beats.summary: Margaret is taken home, and her father is shocked to learn what she did.

beats.scene: Mr Thornton stands at the Hales' front door with his hat in his hand
beats.summary: The next morning Mr Thornton calls to ask after Margaret's wound.

beats.scene: Mr Thornton speaks earnestly to Margaret in the little parlour
beats.summary: Mr Thornton tells Margaret that he loves her and asks her to marry him.

beats.scene: Margaret turns away from him with a cold, proud face
beats.summary: Margaret believes he speaks out of gratitude, and she refuses him coldly.

beats.scene: Margaret sits alone by a window, trembling and pale
beats.summary: After he leaves, Margaret is shaken, though she tells herself she feels nothing.

beats.scene: Mrs Thornton sits upright and angry in her stiff parlour
beats.summary: Mrs Thornton learns of the refusal and is furious that anyone would reject her son.

beats.scene: A thin queue of men stands outside a mill gate in the cold
beats.summary: Hunger breaks the strike, and some of the men begin to give in.

beats.scene: Margaret visits Higgins, who sits stubbornly by a cold fireplace
beats.summary: Higgins refuses to give in, though his family is going hungry.

beats.scene: A crowd of workers walks back through the mill gates with bowed heads
beats.summary: The strike collapses, and the men return to work on the masters' terms.

beats.scene: Margaret watches the town from her window with a troubled face
beats.summary: Margaret regrets her words to Mr Thornton and wonders why she cannot forget him.

beats.scene: Margaret sits beside a narrow bed where Bessy lies thin and pale
beats.summary: Bessy grows weaker, and Margaret visits her every day.

beats.scene: Bessy turns her face toward Margaret on a worn pillow
beats.summary: Bessy talks quietly of her life and thanks Margaret for her friendship.

beats.scene: Margaret reads from a worn Bible while evening light fills the room
beats.summary: At Bessy's request Margaret reads once more from the last book of the Bible.

beats.scene: Bessy holds Margaret's hand tightly and speaks in a whisper
beats.summary: Bessy asks Margaret to look after her father and to be kind to him.

beats.scene: A candle burns beside the bed as Bessy lies very still
beats.summary: Bessy dies at dusk with Margaret at her side.

beats.scene: Higgins stands in the doorway of the small kitchen, staring at the bed
beats.summary: Higgins comes home to find that his daughter has died, and his grief is terrible.

beats.scene: Margaret walks home alone through dark, wet streets of Milton
beats.summary: Margaret returns home late, tearful and exhausted, thinking of Bessy and her father.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale lies back on her pillows and looks at Margaret with longing
beats.summary: Mrs Hale, growing weaker, tells Margaret that she longs to see her son Frederick once more.

beats.scene: Mr Hale and Dixon talk anxiously in a dim hallway
beats.summary: Mr Hale and Dixon fear the danger, but Mrs Hale pleads for her son.

beats.scene: Margaret writes a letter at a desk as her mother lies in bed
beats.summary: Margaret decides to write to Frederick, knowing that the visit will be dangerous.

beats.scene: Margaret waits at a window for a letter from abroad
beats.summary: Margaret waits anxiously for a reply, and at last a letter arrives.

beats.scene: Mr Hale and Dixon prepare a small back room for a secret guest
beats.summary: The family prepares a quiet room for Frederick and agrees to tell nobody.

beats.scene: A tall, tanned young man steps through a dark doorway into Margaret's arms
beats.summary: Frederick arrives secretly at night, and Margaret greets him with joy.

beats.scene: Frederick kneels beside his mother's bed while she touches his face
beats.summary: Mrs Hale is overjoyed to see her son again.

beats.scene: Frederick talks to his father and sister by a small lamp
beats.summary: Frederick tells how a cruel captain drove his men to mutiny on the ship Orion.

beats.scene: Margaret and Frederick laugh together over a late supper in the kitchen
beats.summary: For a few days the house is happy, and Mrs Hale seems almost well.

beats.scene: Dixon peers through the curtains at the street as Frederick sits near the window
beats.summary: Dixon fears that someone will see Frederick, and Margaret warns him to be careful.

beats.scene: Dr Donaldson shakes his head quietly in the hall beside Margaret
beats.summary: Mrs Hale grows suddenly weaker, and the doctor warns that the end is near.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale holds her children's hands on either side of her bed
beats.summary: Mrs Hale speaks tenderly to her children and asks them to look after their father.

beats.scene: A clock ticks in a silent room as the family sits around a bed
beats.summary: Mrs Hale falls asleep, and the family waits through the night.

beats.scene: Margaret and Frederick sit silently at a bedside in the grey dawn light
beats.summary: Mrs Hale dies peacefully at dawn with her children beside her.

beats.scene: Mr Hale weeps at a fresh grave as Margaret holds his arm
beats.summary: Mr Hale is crushed by grief, and Mrs Hale is buried in Milton.

beats.scene: Margaret and Frederick whisper together in a dim hallway beside a travelling bag
beats.summary: Frederick must leave at once, and Margaret insists on seeing him to the station.

beats.scene: A brother and sister walk arm in arm along a gas-lit street at night
beats.summary: The two walk through the lamplit streets, trying to look like any ordinary couple.

beats.scene: Mr Thornton on a station platform stares at a couple in the shadows
beats.summary: Mr Thornton sees Margaret with a young man at the station and wrongly thinks the worst.

beats.scene: A shabby man peers at Frederick's face beneath a platform lamp
beats.summary: A man named Leonards, an old acquaintance, recognises Frederick and threatens to give him up.

beats.scene: Two men struggle together on the edge of a railway platform
beats.summary: Frederick pushes the man away, and the man falls heavily to the ground.

beats.scene: Frederick leaps into a moving train as Margaret stands alone
beats.summary: Frederick escapes on the departing train.

beats.scene: A fallen man lies groaning while a small crowd gathers on the platform
beats.summary: Margaret slips away, shaken, while the injured man is helped by the crowd.

beats.scene: Margaret climbs the dark stairs of her house, one hand on the rail
beats.summary: Margaret reaches home alone, weeping and frightened for her brother and for the injured man.

beats.summary: The man who fell at the station has died, and an inspector comes to the Hales' house.

beats.summary: The inspector asks whether Margaret was at the station that evening.

beats.scene: Margaret lifts her chin and answers in a clear voice
beats.summary: Margaret tells the first lie of her life and says that she was at home.

beats.scene: The inspector closes his notebook and bows politely to Margaret
beats.summary: The inspector accepts her word and leaves, and Margaret trembles with shame and fear.

beats.summary: Margaret is ashamed of her lie and does not understand why Mr Thornton was cold to her.

beats.summary: Higgins takes in Boucher's three children, although he never liked their father.

beats.summary: Higgins is blacklisted by the masters, and food is short in his house.

beats.summary: Higgins swallows his pride and goes to Mr Thornton's mill to ask for work.

beats.summary: Thornton and Higgins talk openly as men for the first time.

beats.summary: Thornton starts a cheap dining room for his workers, and it begins to heal the town's mistrust.

beats.scene: Higgins tells Margaret his news in the Hales' sunlit parlour
beats.summary: Higgins tells Margaret that he has found work with Thornton, and she is glad.

beats.summary: Mr Hale decides to go to Oxford and leaves Margaret at home.

beats.summary: Mr Hale dies suddenly and peacefully in Oxford.

beats.summary: Margaret travels to Oxford and learns that her father is dead.

beats.summary: Margaret is left without parents, and Mr Bell advises her to live with her aunt in London.

beats.summary: Margaret arrives in Harley Street in mourning, and her aunt welcomes her warmly.

beats.summary: Margaret has a quiet room of her own, but she feels numb and far from home.

beats.summary: The dinners and visits of London seem empty to Margaret after the troubles of Milton.

beats.summary: Margaret's thoughts keep returning to Milton: to Higgins, to Bessy and to the mill bell.

beats.summary: Henry Lennox, now a friend, dines at Harley Street and treats Margaret with kindness.

beats.summary: Margaret thinks of Mr Thornton and wonders whether she misjudged him.

A1A2: Margaret Hale was in London, helping her cousin Edith with a dress.
Edith was very happy and talked all day about Captain Lennox.
Margaret lived in her aunt's big house, but she missed the country.
Henry Lennox, the Captain's brother, came to visit the family one afternoon.
Henry and Margaret talked about the country, and her face became bright.
On the wedding day, Edith looked beautiful in white at the church.
After church, everyone ate a big meal and drank to the new couple.
Edith and her husband drove away, and Aunt Shaw cried a little.
The house was very quiet, and Margaret felt alone and a little sad.
Margaret took the train home to her mother and father in Helstone.
The Hales' house at Helstone was small and covered with pink roses.
Margaret and her father walked through the village and visited the poor families.
Her mother was often tired, and she sat quietly in the sunny room.
One warm day, Henry Lennox arrived at the gate with a small bag.
Henry and Mr Hale talked about books, and Margaret showed him the village.
They walked together under tall trees, and Margaret felt a little worried.
In the garden, Henry said he loved her and wanted to marry her.
Margaret did not love him, so she said no in a kind voice.
Henry looked sad and angry, and he left Helstone the next day.
Margaret felt glad, but she saw that her father looked very worried.
At supper, Mr Hale was quiet, and Margaret thought something was wrong.
Mr Hale told his daughter that he could not stay in the church.
He said he had doubts, and nothing could change his mind now.
Margaret saw that they would lose their home and their quiet life.
Her father was afraid to tell her mother, so Margaret did it.
Mrs Hale cried, and Dixon was very angry with Mr Hale's choice.
Mr Hale wrote a letter to the bishop and then one to Mr Bell.
Mr Bell wrote back, and he said Mr Hale could teach in Milton.
Milton was a big town with many mills, and Margaret felt afraid.
Mr Hale made up his mind, and the family started to pack.
Margaret walked once more through the forest and said goodbye to everyone.
On Sunday, the villagers cried as Mr Hale spoke in church for the last time.
The house was empty now, and Mrs Hale was too ill to travel.
Margaret and her father took the train north, and the hills grew grey.
From the train, Margaret saw Milton under a thick cloud of black smoke.
In the street, tired women in warm cloths hurried past, and they spoke strangely.
The man showed them many houses, but they were too big or too dirty.
At last they found a small house that was cheap enough for them.
Margaret hung up curtains and put the books on shelves in the small room.
Her mother arrived tired and sad, and the first night was very noisy.
Every morning there was black dust on the windows, and Dixon was angry.
Mrs Hale lay in bed and talked all day about the roses at home.
Mr Hale put his books on the table and looked forward to teaching.
Margaret walked through the streets and saw carts, canals and tall grey buildings.
At noon a bell rang, and hundreds of workers ran out into the road.
Some girls spoke to Margaret, and one of them touched her warm coat.
Her father said the workers were called hands, and he spoke of Mr Thornton.
Dixon came home from the market with a full basket and many complaints.
Margaret looked after the money and learned how carefully they must spend it.
That night, Margaret lay awake and wondered what Mr Thornton was like.
Mr Thornton came to the house, tall and dark, and he bowed stiffly.
He wanted to learn Greek, so Mr Hale began to read Homer with him.
Margaret said she did not like trade, and Mr Thornton was proud and angry.
Mr Hale liked his new pupil, and Margaret heard them talk happily.
Mrs Thornton visited the Hales, and she looked at Margaret with cold eyes.
The Hales visited the mill, and Margaret saw the huge building for the first time.
Mrs Thornton's sitting room was neat and stiff, and she loved her son very much.
Fanny Thornton asked Margaret about London clothes and talked for a long time.
Margaret watched Mr Thornton in the yard, and his workers seemed afraid of him.
On the way home, Margaret said she disliked him, but her father did not agree.
Margaret met a thin girl named Bessy, who was coughing badly.
Bessy said the cotton dust in the mill had made her very ill.
Margaret visited Bessy's home, and it was small, poor and very clean.
Nicholas Higgins came home and spoke plainly about the masters.
He did not trust ladies, but Margaret spoke to him honestly.
Margaret read from the Bible, and Bessy loved the last book.
Mr Hale came to visit Higgins, and the two men talked about God.
Higgins said the workers might stop work to ask for better pay.
Mrs Hale grew weaker, and Dixon did not like Margaret's visits.
Margaret saw two different worlds in Milton, and she wanted to know both.
Mr Thornton told them how his father died and left the family poor.
Margaret listened quietly, and she was touched by his story.
Soon, the Hales were asked to dinner at the Thorntons' big house.
The table was full of silver and rich food, and the guests ate well.
Some masters said that workers must always do as they are told.
They spoke of their workers as if they were children, and Margaret was angry.
After dinner, Margaret told Mr Thornton that he was too hard on his men.
He answered that a master must be free to run his own mill.
The talk ended coldly, and Mrs Thornton and Fanny saw the tension.
At home, Margaret felt sorry, and Mr Thornton could not forget her.
Margaret read a letter from her brother Frederick, and she kept it secret.
Frederick had joined a mutiny against a cruel captain, so he could not come home.
The doctor visited Mrs Hale and said that she was very ill.
Trade was bad, and the masters agreed to keep wages low.
Higgins told Margaret that the men would stop work if nobody listened.
The workers put down their tools, and the mills became silent.
Food ran out in the poor streets, and Boucher's children were hungry.
Mr Thornton refused to change his mind and sent for Irish workers.
Margaret asked him not to do it, but he said it was necessary.
Boucher made the angry men more angry, and Higgins was afraid.
The Irish workers came by train, and the strikers watched them angrily.
The crowd grew large, and Higgins tried to make the men calm.
Margaret went to the Thorntons' house, and she found a crowd outside.
The mob threw stones at the windows, and the family hid inside.
Margaret told Mr Thornton to speak to them before the soldiers came.
Mr Thornton went out alone, and Margaret followed him quickly.
Margaret put her arms around him, and a stone hit her head.
The crowd saw her blood, and they grew quiet and stepped back.
Soldiers marched in, the crowd ran away, and the yard was quiet.
They carried Margaret inside, and Mrs Thornton looked at her coldly.
Margaret was taken home, and her father was shocked by what she did.
The next morning, Mr Thornton came to ask about her head.
He told her that he loved her and asked her to marry him.
She thought he only felt thankful, so she said no in a cold voice.
After he left, Margaret shook, but she told herself she felt nothing.
Mrs Thornton heard the news and was angry that Margaret had refused her son.
The strike was breaking, because the men and their children were hungry.
Higgins would not give in, even though his family had no food.
The strike ended, and the men went back to work on the masters' terms.
Margaret was sorry for her words, and she could not stop thinking of him.
Bessy grew weaker, and Margaret came to see her every day.
Bessy spoke quietly about her life and thanked Margaret for her kindness.
At the end of the day, Margaret read from the Bible again.
Bessy held her hand and asked her to be kind to Higgins.
At dusk, Bessy died, and Margaret was at her side.
Higgins came home and saw that his daughter was dead, and he cried.
Margaret walked home through the dark, wet streets and could not stop crying.
Mrs Hale said she wanted to see her son Frederick before she died.
Mr Hale and Dixon were afraid, but Mrs Hale begged for her son.
Margaret sat down to write to Frederick, and she knew it was dangerous.
Margaret waited for a reply, and at last a letter came.
The family made a quiet room for Frederick and told nobody.
Frederick came in the dark of night, and Margaret held him close.
Mrs Hale was full of joy to see her son again.
Frederick told them about his ship and the cruel captain.
For a few days the house was happy, and Mrs Hale seemed better.
Dixon was afraid that someone would see Frederick, and Margaret warned him.
Mrs Hale grew weak, and the doctor said the end was near.
Mrs Hale spoke kindly to her children and asked them to look after their father.
Mrs Hale fell asleep, and the family waited all night beside her.
At dawn, Mrs Hale died quietly with her children beside her.
Mr Hale was broken by grief, and his wife was buried in Milton.
Frederick had to leave quickly, and Margaret went with him to the train.
They walked arm in arm through the dark streets, like any young couple.
Mr Thornton saw them at the station and thought the worst.
A man who knew Frederick looked at his face and wanted to stop him.
Frederick pushed the man away, and the man fell down hard.
Frederick jumped on the train as it moved, and he was gone.
The man lay on the ground, and Margaret hurried away from the crowd.
Margaret came home alone, and she cried because she was afraid.
The man at the station had died, and an inspector came to the house.
The inspector asked Margaret if she was at the station that night.
Margaret told the first lie of her life and said she was at home.
The inspector believed her and left, and Margaret shook with fear and shame.
Mr Thornton heard that she had lied, and he said nothing.
Margaret was ashamed of her lie, and she did not know why he was so cold.
Boucher was found drowned in a stream, and the town was shocked.
Higgins took in Boucher's three children, although he never liked their father.
The masters would not hire Higgins, and there was little food at home.
Higgins went to Mr Thornton's mill and asked him for work.
Mr Thornton heard Higgins's honest words and gave him a job.
Thornton and Higgins talked openly, like two men, for the first time.
Thornton started a cheap kitchen for his workers, and trust began to grow.
Higgins told Margaret he had found work, and she was glad.
Mr Bell visited Milton and asked Mr Hale to come to Oxford.
Mr Hale decided to go, and Margaret stayed at home.
In Oxford, Mr Hale visited his old friends and enjoyed the old college.
Mr Hale sat quietly in a garden chair, and then he died.
Margaret went to Oxford and found that her father was dead.
Margaret had no parents now, and Mr Bell told her to go to London.
Margaret came to her aunt's house in London, and she wore black clothes.
She had a quiet room, but she felt empty and far from home.
Edith was back from Corfu with her baby, and she talked and talked.
The London dinners and visits seemed empty to Margaret after Milton.
Margaret often thought of Milton, Higgins, Bessy and the loud mill bell.
Henry Lennox came to dinner, and he was kind to Margaret.
Margaret walked alone in a park and thought about Mr Thornton.
Henry said it had been a bad year, and some mills were in trouble.
Mr Thornton worked late at night and tried to save his business.
Mr Bell wrote to ask Margaret to go with him to Helstone.
Margaret and Mr Bell rode south, and she grew happier with every mile.
At Helstone, the village looked different, and strangers lived in her old home.
She visited old friends and saw that many things had changed.
Mr Bell became ill at the village inn, and Margaret looked after him.
Mr Bell spoke of Mr Hale and said he wanted to help Margaret.
Mr Bell went back to Oxford, and Margaret went back to London.
Some weeks later, Margaret heard that Mr Bell had died.
Mr Bell left Margaret his money and the buildings of the mill.
Henry Lennox helped Margaret and told her that Mr Thornton was her tenant.
Henry told her that Mr Thornton was in trouble, and Margaret asked for his advice.
A large order failed, and Mr Thornton could not pay his debts.
Mr Thornton told his workers that the mill must close, and they left silently.
Higgins stood alone in the yard and felt sorry for his master.
Mrs Thornton sat proud and still as the family lost almost everything.
Thornton went to London to find help, and he met Henry Lennox.
Henry told him that Miss Hale owned the mill buildings.
Thornton asked about the man at the station, and Henry said, “Her brother.”
Thornton was full of regret, and he decided to go and see her.
They met in London, and they both felt shy and stiff.
Thornton said he must leave Milton, and he thanked her for helping Higgins.
Margaret held out a folded paper and offered to lend him money.
Mr Thornton said no, because he was too proud to take her money.
Margaret said it was good business, and the workers needed the mill.
Mr Thornton looked away, then he smiled, and he said yes.
They talked about the night at the station, and each asked to be forgiven.
He asked if she could ever love him, and she only smiled.
She said she loved him, and he kissed her.
Aunt Shaw was very happy, and Henry Lennox took the news kindly.
The mill opened again, and Thornton and Higgins worked side by side.
Margaret and John Thornton were married, and the north and south became friends.
B1B2: It is the day before Edith Shaw's wedding, and the drawing room in Harley Street is full of silk and flowers. Margaret Hale, her quiet cousin, kneels on the carpet to pin the hem of the dress.

Edith lies on the sofa with her eyes half closed, talking about Captain Lennox and the places his regiment will take him. Margaret listens kindly, although she has heard every story many times already.
Margaret came to Harley Street as a young girl, and her aunt has been generous to her ever since. Even so, the dinners, the visits and the endless gossip have never felt like home to her.
That afternoon Henry Lennox, the Captain's younger brother, calls at the house to see the bride. He is a young lawyer with a quick mind and a friendly, teasing way of speaking.
Henry asks Margaret where she would rather be, and she answers at once that she would be at Helstone. Her face lights up as she describes the forest and the village, and he watches her with interest.
On the wedding day the church is full, and Edith walks up the aisle smiling like a girl at a party. Margaret stands behind her, serious and a little tearful, as the Captain takes his bride's hand.
At the wedding breakfast the guests drink to the happy couple, and the room is loud with laughter. Henry Lennox finds a place near Margaret and says he hopes to visit her in Hampshire.
By the afternoon Edith and her husband are on their way, and their carriage is covered in white ribbons. Aunt Shaw cries into her handkerchief, and the large house suddenly seems very empty.
That night Margaret sorts her few belongings and thinks about her years in London. She is glad to have been useful, but she cannot wait to be with her parents again.
The next morning she takes the train south, and the town gives way to fields and hedges. By the time she reaches Hampshire she is smiling at every cottage and every cow.
The Hales' vicarage at Helstone is small and low, and its walls are covered with roses. Margaret's father and mother come out to meet her, and old Dixon, the servant, is close behind them.

In the mornings Margaret walks with her father through the village, and the cottagers greet her by name. She has missed their cheerful faces, and she listens patiently to every long story about their children.
Mrs Hale spends most of the day on the sofa, because her health has never been strong. She tells Margaret that she often wishes for the comfortable life she had when she was young.
A few days later Henry Lennox arrives at the vicarage gate with a small bag in his hand. Mr Hale, who is always glad of a scholar's company, welcomes him warmly and offers him a room.
In the study Henry and Mr Hale talk happily about books and ideas for hours at a time. When the talk ends, Margaret takes Henry out to see the lanes and the old trees she loves best.
One afternoon they walk for a long time beneath the great trees of the forest. Margaret begins to notice that Henry is quieter than usual, and she feels uneasy without quite knowing why.
Later that week he finds her alone among the roses and tells her, in a serious voice, that he loves her. He asks her to be his wife, and he waits anxiously for her reply.
Margaret has never thought of him in that way, and she does not pretend that she has. She thanks him for his kindness and says no, although she can see that her answer hurts him deeply.
Henry bows stiffly and says that he will not trouble her again, though he does not promise to forget her. He leaves the vicarage early the next morning, and the house seems quiet after his going.

Margaret sits in the garden as the evening light fades, relieved and a little ashamed to feel so. At supper she notices that her father hardly eats and keeps looking at her, as if he has something heavy to say.
Mr Hale sits at the supper table without speaking, and his tea grows cold in front of him. Margaret watches his tired face and feels sure that something serious is on his mind.
The next afternoon her father asks her to walk with him along the lane. He tells her quietly that he has been troubled by doubts for a long time and must now leave the Church.
He does not ask for her advice, and she can see that he has already thought about it for many sleepless nights. She says only that she will stand by him, and he presses her hand in silence.
As they walk back, Margaret begins to understand what this will mean. They will lose the vicarage, the garden, the income and the whole peaceful life she has loved since she was a child.
Mr Hale confesses that he does not have the courage to tell his wife herself, so he begs Margaret to do it. She sits beside her mother that evening and chooses her words as gently as she can.

Mrs Hale is stunned, and then she weeps bitterly, for she has always dreaded change. Dixon, who has served the family for years, declares that her master has no right to bring such trouble on his wife.

Mr Hale writes to the bishop to give up his place, and the letter takes him the whole of one long evening. Then he writes to his old friend Mr Bell in Oxford, asking what a man like him can do in the world.
Mr Bell's reply arrives within the week, and it is kind and full of good sense. He says that Mr Hale could earn a living by teaching private pupils in Milton, a busy manufacturing town in the north.

Margaret reads the description aloud to her parents, and her voice falters at the words about smoke and crowds. She tries to sound cheerful for her mother's sake, although she cannot imagine how anyone could live there.

After a few days of anxious talk, Mr Hale makes up his mind to go. The family fixes a date, the cases are brought down from the attic, and Helstone begins to feel like a place they are already leaving.

In her last week at Helstone, Margaret walks to every place she loves, and she says goodbye to each cottage and tree. The cottagers bring small gifts, and some of the old women cry as they hold her hands.
On the last Sunday the little church is full, and Mr Hale preaches to his people for the final time. Many of them are in tears, and he can scarcely finish the service.

Dixon packs the china and the books into crates, grumbling all the while about the north. Mrs Hale is too weak to make the journey yet, so Margaret and her father agree to travel ahead and find a house.
The train carries them north through the long day, and the soft green fields gradually give way to flat, grey land. Margaret watches from the window and thinks how far she is from home.

Towards evening they see a heavy cloud of smoke lying over the horizon, and Mr Hale tells her that it hangs above Milton. As the train comes closer she sees tall chimneys and rows of black roofs pressed together.

The streets are packed with workers hurrying home, the women in shawls and the men in rough clothes. Margaret has never heard such loud, blunt speech, and she is surprised to find that she does not feel afraid.
A house agent shows them a row of houses, but the good ones are far too grand and the cheap ones are dirty and damp. Mr Hale has little money, and the day ends without any success.

At last they choose a plain brick house at Crampton, on the edge of the town, with small rooms and windows blackened by smoke. Margaret smiles and says it will do, although her heart sinks as she steps inside.

For the next few days Margaret scrubs, hangs curtains and arranges her father's books on the shelves. She even finds a corner for a vase of flowers, and the small parlour begins to look almost welcoming.

Mrs Hale arrives with Dixon in a hired carriage, pale and tired after the long journey. That night the whole family lies awake listening to the clatter of the town, and nobody speaks of how strange it feels.

Every morning the windowsills of the little house at Crampton are covered with a fine layer of black soot. Dixon wipes them with a furious cloth and declares that nobody could stay clean in such a place.

Mrs Hale spends most of her days in bed, and she talks constantly about the roses and the green lanes of Helstone. Margaret sits beside her and listens, though she knows that each memory makes her mother sadder.

Mr Hale, on the other hand, is almost cheerful, for he has put out his books and written to several families. He tells his daughter that the town is full of interesting people and that he is eager to meet them.

One afternoon Margaret goes out alone, and she walks past warehouses, wagons loaded with cotton and a long, greasy canal. The noise and the hurry are tiring, but she cannot help admiring the energy of the place.

At noon a bell rings loudly from a nearby mill, and hundreds of workers pour into the street. They are laughing, shouting and pushing past each other, and Margaret has to step into a doorway to let them by.

A group of mill girls stops to look at her, and one of them touches her shawl and says it is very fine. Margaret answers kindly, and the girls go off giggling, as pleased as if they had received a gift.

At supper she tells her father about the girls, and he explains that the workers in the mills are called hands. He adds that his old friend Mr Bell has a tenant in Milton named Mr Thornton, who owns a large mill.

Dixon comes back from the market with a heavy basket and a long list of complaints about the prices and the strange way people talk. She insists that she will never get used to the north, but she buys the best vegetables in the market.

Margaret takes charge of the household accounts, and she soon discovers that every penny must be counted. She keeps her mother's meals simple and her father's study warm, and she wastes nothing at all.

At supper one evening Mr Hale announces that Mr Thornton has asked to become his first pupil. That night Margaret stands at her window watching the mill lamps glow in the dark, wondering what sort of man a mill owner can be.

Mr Thornton arrives for his first lesson at the Hales' house, a tall, dark man with a strong face and a stiff manner. He bows to Margaret without smiling, and she thinks him proud, while he privately thinks the same of her.

He has had little schooling, he explains to Mr Hale, but he wants to learn the great poets of Greece. They open the Iliad together, and Mr Thornton reads each line with the determination of a man climbing a hill.

While Margaret pours the tea, the talk turns to trade, and she remarks with a little scorn that she dislikes anything to do with shops. Mr Thornton replies calmly that the cloth she is wearing was made by the work of the north, and he does not seem pleased.

After a few weeks Mr Hale and his pupil have become real friends, and the lessons last long past their hour. Margaret hears their voices from the next room and is quietly surprised at how much her father enjoys them.

Soon afterwards Mrs Thornton comes to call at Crampton, a stern, grey-haired woman in a plain black dress. She is perfectly polite, but she looks at Margaret as if she were weighing her, and Margaret feels her cold judgement.

A week later the Hales return the visit at Marlborough Mills, where the Thorntons live beside the mill itself. Margaret stops in the yard to look up at the long building, with its many lit windows and its heavy, steady hum.
Mrs Thornton's parlour is neat and formal, with every chair covered and every ornament in its place. Margaret soon sees that its owner lives for her son and thinks no honour too great for him.

Fanny Thornton, the daughter, is a pretty and talkative girl who wants to hear about London fashions. Margaret answers her politely, and she is surprised to find that she likes Fanny more than she expected.

From the yard Margaret sees Mr Thornton crossing among his workers, and she notices how they touch their caps and drop their eyes. They seem to respect him, and she suspects they are also a little afraid of him.
Walking home, Margaret tells her father that she does not like the mill owner at all. Mr Hale answers that Mr Thornton is honest and sincere, and that she will be wrong to judge him by his manners.

On a walk through the poorer streets, Margaret meets a thin, pale girl who is coughing at a corner. The girl says her name is Bessy Higgins and that her younger sister Mary is waiting for her at home.

Bessy sits down on a doorstep to rest and tells Margaret that she works in the carding room of a mill. The fine cotton fluff fills her chest like smoke, she says calmly, and she does not expect to live much longer.

Margaret asks if she may visit, and Bessy agrees, so the next day Margaret climbs the narrow stairs to the Higgins house. The kitchen is small and the furniture is poor, but the floor is scrubbed and the fire burns brightly.

Bessy's father, Nicholas Higgins, comes home from the mill, a broad, bearded man with a direct eye and a rough voice. He tells Margaret plainly that the masters care nothing for the workers, who are valued only for their strength.
Higgins says that ladies usually come only to preach and then go away again. Margaret answers that she has come simply to see Bessy and cannot judge the masters yet, and he looks at her with respect.

On later visits Margaret reads to Bessy from the Bible, and the sick girl asks her always for the last book. She loves its promise of a city where there will be no pain, no tears and no more hard work.

One evening Mr Hale comes to the Higgins house with his daughter, and he and Nicholas talk by the fire about faith and doubt. Higgins admits that he cannot believe as his daughter does, and Mr Hale, who knows his own doubts, listens kindly.

On the street Margaret sees groups of men talking quietly at the corner, and Higgins tells her that the workers have a Union. He says that if the masters cut wages, the men will stop work together, and nothing will make them go back until they are heard.
At home Mrs Hale grows weaker, and Margaret nurses her faithfully at night after her visits. Dixon tells her sharply that a clergyman's daughter has no need to spend her days among mill families.

One evening Margaret stands at the window and looks out across the dark rooftops of Milton. She sees that the masters and the workers live in two different worlds, and she tells herself that she must try to understand them both.

One evening Mr Thornton stays to talk by the fire, and he tells the Hales how he came to be a master. His father died when he was a boy and left the family in debt, and he left school at fifteen to work in a shop.

He says that he and his mother lived on almost nothing for years, and that he saved every penny he could. Margaret listens in silence, and although she does not say so, she is moved by his plain, unboasting voice.

Mrs Hale grows weaker, and Mr Hale sends for Dr Donaldson, who listens to her chest with a serious face. Afterwards the doctor tells Margaret quietly that her mother is more ill than the family has admitted.

Margaret hears rumours of the plan and goes at once to speak to him. She begs him to think of the anger it will cause, but he replies that it is the only way to keep his mill alive.

That night Margaret stands at her window, wishing she had spoken more gently to Mr Thornton. She cannot say why she thinks of his face so often, and she does not dare to look for the answer.
Bessy grows weaker every day, and Margaret sits beside her narrow bed for hours at a time. Mary has gone to work, and the little house is very quiet.

The clock ticks in the silent room as the family sits around the bed, and nobody wants to leave. Mrs Hale falls into a deep sleep, and Margaret and Frederick wait beside her through the long hours of the night.

A message brings the news to Margaret, and she travels to Oxford at once. She stands in her dark dress outside the college gate, and she cannot go in, because she cannot believe it is true.

Margaret is given a pretty room of her own with a view of the quiet street, but she feels numb and far away. She puts away her few things and sits for a long time with her hands in her lap.

Edith has come home from Corfu with a small baby, and she lies on the sofa talking happily about the voyage and the heat. Margaret listens in silence, glad that her cousin is content, but she cannot join in the talk.

Every evening there are visitors, and Margaret sits in the drawing room among the lamps and flowers and the polite conversation. After the troubles and hard truths of Milton, the dinners and calls of London seem small and hollow.

One wet afternoon Margaret stands at the window and watches the rain fall on the square. She finds herself thinking again of Higgins and of Bessy, and even of the loud mill bell and the smoky streets.

Henry Lennox comes to dinner, and he treats Margaret with perfect kindness and not a trace of resentment. They talk easily, like old friends, and she is grateful that her refusal has not spoiled their friendship.
Alone in the park beneath the dripping trees, Margaret thinks about Mr Thornton. She remembers his proposal and her cold answer, and for the first time she wonders whether she misjudged him.

One evening Henry shows her a newspaper folded at a column about trade, and he says that the cotton business has had a hard year. Several of the mills in the north are in trouble, he adds, and Margaret feels a quick stab of fear.

At Helstone she stands beneath the old oak and looks around the village, but much is different. New people live in the vicarage now, and the garden has been changed, and she feels like a stranger in her own home.
She walks through the village and visits the cottagers, and some of them cry when they see her. Many of the old faces are gone, and the lanes that seemed so large in her memory feel small and quiet.
Mr Bell is tired by the journey, and one evening he becomes so ill that he must stay in bed at the village inn. Margaret nurses him for several days, and she is glad to be useful.

As he lies on a heap of pillows, Mr Bell speaks quietly of his old friend, Mr Hale, and of their youth together in Oxford. He says that he wants to see Margaret provided for, and she is touched, though she does not think much of it.

As soon as Mr Bell is strong enough to travel, a carriage takes him back to Oxford, and Margaret waves goodbye from the inn. She returns to Harley Street, but she does not feel that the old man has recovered.

A great order fails at the worst possible moment, and the ledger on Mr Thornton's desk shows that he cannot pay what he owes. For weeks he has tried every way to save the mill, but in the end there is nothing left to try.
One morning Mr Thornton calls his workers into the yard and tells them quietly that the mill must close. They leave in silence, and the gate is shut behind them for the last time.
Higgins stands alone in the empty yard and looks back at the closed gate. He is sorry for the master who gave him a chance, and he wonders what will happen to the town without him.

Mrs Thornton sits upright in her stiff parlour while the furniture is covered with cloths. She does not complain or weep, and she says only that she has faced hard times before and can face them again.

Mr Thornton goes to London to ask for help, and he must see a lawyer named Henry Lennox on a business matter. He waits in the office with his hat on his knee, and he does not know whom he is about to meet.

Hesitating, Thornton asks about a young man he once saw with Miss Hale at the station. Henry replies that it must have been her brother, a sailor who came home in secret when their mother was dying.
Mr Thornton leaves the office like a man in a dream and walks along the London street, deep in thought. He sees now that he has misjudged her in the cruellest way, and he feels a bitter regret.
On an impulse Mr Thornton goes to Harley Street and is shown into the drawing room, where Margaret rises in surprise. They greet each other formally, and both of them feel shy and stiff.
Mr Thornton tells Margaret that he must leave Milton, and he thanks her for her kindness to Higgins and his family. He bows and says that he must go, but he does not seem to want to move.
Margaret takes a folded paper from her bag and holds it out across the table. She tells Mr Thornton that she wishes to lend him money from her fortune, so that he can save his mill.
Mr Thornton stands stiffly with his hands behind his back and says that he cannot take her money. His pride is as strong as ever, and he cannot bear the thought of owing so much to her.

Aunt Shaw claps her hands with delight when she hears the news, and she begins at once to plan a party. Henry Lennox bows to Margaret with a polite smile and wishes her every happiness, as a true friend should.
