Margaret stands quite still on the sandy path, with the whole familiar lane seeming to tilt beneath her feet.

He does not ask for her counsel, and she soon sees that his decision has been made through many sleepless nights and cannot be shaken by anything she might say. She offers instead the only thing she has, her loyalty, and tells him that wherever he goes she will go with him. He presses her hand without a word, and his eyes are bright with gratitude and shame.

Walking home, Margaret begins to measure what this resolution will cost them: the vicarage, the garden, the modest but certain income and the whole gentle rhythm of a life she has loved since childhood. She feels no anger, only a sorrowful astonishment that so quiet a man should have been driven by his conscience to so great an upheaval. The roses along the garden wall seem suddenly to belong to someone else, and she cannot bear to look at them.

Mr Hale confesses that he has not the courage to tell his wife, who has never been strong, and he begs Margaret to break the news. That evening she sits beside her mother on the sofa and chooses her words with the greatest care, knowing that every one will fall like a stone. It is the first time she has felt herself to be the stronger of her parents, and the discovery is not a comfortable one.

Mrs Hale is stunned, and then she weeps without restraint, for she has always dreaded change as other women dread illness. Dixon, who has served the family faithfully for many years and has listened at the door, declares that her master has no right to bring such trouble upon a delicate wife. Margaret, between them, is left to soothe the one and to silence the other, and she does both with a calm that surprises her.

Mr Hale gives up his living in a letter to the bishop that costs him the whole of a long evening, each sentence written and rewritten until it seems to say exactly what he means. When it is sealed, he writes a second letter, to his old friend Mr Bell at Oxford, asking what is to become of a man who has made himself unfit for his only profession. The lamp burns low as he writes, and Margaret, watching from the doorway, thinks he has never looked so tired or so free.

Mr Bell's reply comes within the week, and it is kind, blunt and sensible, as his letters always are. He declares that a scholar of Mr Hale's learning can earn a decent living by teaching private pupils, and he suggests Milton, a great manufacturing town in the north where he himself owns property. Margaret reads the words twice before she understands that her father's new life will be spent in the very kind of place she has always been taught to avoid.

That night she reads aloud from a guidebook to her parents, and her voice falters at the passages about smoke, noise and crowded streets. Mrs Hale shudders, and Mr Hale, anxious to be cheerful, says that men and women live very happily in such places and that the town is said to be full of energy. Margaret nods and smiles, determined that her mother shall never guess how deep her own dismay goes.

After several days of anxious talk and little sleep, Mr Hale declares that the matter is settled and that they will go north before the leaves begin to turn. The date is fixed, the empty cases are carried down from the attic, and a bustling kind of sadness settles over the house. Already Helstone seems to Margaret like a place she is looking at from a train window, loved and lovely and quickly receding.

In her last week at Helstone, Margaret walks to every corner of the parish as if she were committing it to memory: the mossy bridge, the great oak on the common, the cottage gardens bright with late flowers. The old women press her hands and give her little bunches of herbs, and she is surprised by how hard it is to say a cheerful goodbye. She knows she will remember each of these faces long after she has forgotten the names.

On the last Sunday the little church is crowded to the doors, and Mr Hale preaches to his people for the final time in a voice that shakes whenever he lifts his eyes from the page. There is hardly a dry face in the pews, and Margaret, sitting by her mother, fixes her gaze on a patch of coloured light on the floor lest she should break down. When the service is over at last, nobody in the crowded church wants to be the first to leave, and they linger long in the porch.

Dixon packs the china, the linen and her master's precious books into wooden crates, grumbling the whole time about the heathen north and its smoky ways. Mrs Hale, worn out by the strain of departure, is too unwell to make the journey at once, and it is agreed that Margaret and her father shall go ahead to find a house. Before she goes, Margaret kisses her mother goodbye and promises to write to her every single day until they meet again.

The train carries father and daughter northward through the long afternoon, and the soft hedged fields of the south give way by degrees to flatter, barer country under a heavier sky. Margaret leans against the window and watches the landscape slide away, conscious that each mile is carrying her further from everything she has ever known. Mr Hale dozes with a book on his knee, and she lets him sleep.

Towards evening a dull cloud appears on the horizon, ragged at its edges and lit from beneath with a sullen glow, and Mr Hale tells her quietly that it hangs above Milton. As the train draws nearer she can see the tall chimneys rising in their hundreds, trailing black ribbons of smoke, and the endless roofs pressed together like the scales of some enormous animal. She feels as though she were being carried to the edge of another world.

The streets of the town are thronged with workers hurrying home, the women in shawls and heavy clogs and the men in rough jackets, all talking in a broad, blunt dialect that she can scarcely follow. Nobody steps aside for her, nobody lowers his voice, and nobody appears to care in the least that she is a stranger. To her own surprise, she finds the vigour of the crowd more exciting than frightening.

A house agent leads them from street to street, and the houses he shows are either so grand that Mr Hale's small savings would not last a year or so dismal that Margaret can hardly cross the threshold. Walls are streaked with damp, windows are grimed with soot, and every landlord seems to expect the rent in advance. The long day ends with aching feet, a headache and no result whatever to show for all their trouble.

At last they settle on a plain brick house at Crampton, on the outskirts of the town, whose rooms are small and whose windows are tinted grey by the smoke. Margaret says brightly that it will do very well, and she means it, for her father is plainly exhausted and her mother needs a roof above all things. Only when she is alone upstairs does she allow herself one long, silent sigh.

For several days she works like a servant, scrubbing the floors, hanging the curtains and lining her father's books up on the shelves until the shabby parlour begins to take on a look of home. She finds a jug for a few late flowers bought from a street seller, and she puts it on the table where the light is best. Even Mr Hale, who notices little, stops in the doorway to say how pleasant it looks.

Mrs Hale arrives at last with Dixon, in a hired carriage that rattles over the cobbles, and she steps down looking so pale and frail that Margaret's heart contracts. She says nothing of the house or the street, but only asks to lie down, and the family retires early to rest. All night the town clatters and clangs beyond the windows, and not one of them pretends to be asleep.

Every morning a fine layer of black soot has settled on the windowsills of the little house at Crampton, and every morning Dixon attacks it with a furious cloth and an even more furious commentary. She declares that no Christian could be expected to keep a house clean in such a place and that the very air must be made of cinders. Margaret, who has begun to find the black dust a kind of grim joke, says nothing.

Mrs Hale takes to her bed for much of the day, and while the muffled roar of the town goes on outside she talks endlessly of the roses and the green lanes of Helstone. Margaret sits beside her, holding her hand and listening, though she can see that each memory only deepens her mother's sadness. There is no remedy for such a longing, and she has learned that the kindest thing is simply to let it be spoken.

Mr Hale, by contrast, is almost buoyant, for he has arranged his books in the little study, written to several families who might want a tutor and begun to take a scholar's interest in the strangeness of his surroundings. He tells his daughter that a manufacturing town is a living lesson in the energy of the age and that he is eager to meet its people. Margaret is relieved to see him smile, even if the smile owes a good deal to determination.

On the third afternoon Margaret ventures out alone, and she wanders through streets lined with warehouses, past wagons groaning under bales of cotton and along the margin of a canal whose surface shines with oil. The din is tiring and the smoke irritates her eyes, but she cannot help admiring the sheer purposeful busyness of everything she sees. Nothing here is idle, and nothing is merely ornamental, and she finds that the plainness of it all is oddly bracing.

At midday a great bell clangs from a nearby mill, and within moments the doors burst open and hundreds of workers pour into the street in a tide of shawls, caps and clattering clogs. They shout, jostle and laugh with the abandon of children let out of school, and Margaret, who has never seen so many people move together, retreats into a doorway to let them pass. The sound of their voices fills the narrow street like water pouring through a channel, and it is a long while before it fades.

A group of mill girls pauses to stare at the stranger in her good shawl, and one of them, bolder than the rest, reaches out and fingers the fringe, announcing frankly that it is a fine piece. Margaret does not shrink back, but answers them in her friendliest voice, and they go off giggling, delighted as if she had made them a present. It strikes her that these women have none of the timid deference she has been taught to expect from the poor.

At supper she describes the encounter to her father, who explains with a thoughtful nod that the workers in the great mills are known here as hands, a name that seems to him both practical and slightly chilling. He adds that his old friend Mr Bell has a tenant in Milton, a Mr Thornton, who owns one of the largest mills in the town and who has an excellent reputation. Margaret files the name away in her memory without any particular interest, as one does with the names of strangers.

Dixon returns from the market with a heavy basket and a catalogue of grievances, among them the price of butter, the quality of the fish and the incomprehensible speech of the stallholders. She vows that she will never grow accustomed to the north, and yet she has contrived to buy the freshest vegetables in the whole market. Margaret, who has begun to understand the old servant's gruffness, thanks her warmly and sees her stand a little taller.

Margaret takes charge of the household accounts, and she soon discovers that in this town every penny must be counted twice, for coal is dear, rent is high and her father's earnings are as yet no more than a hope. She keeps her mother's meals nourishing, her father's study warm and her own wardrobe carefully mended. It is a lesson in thrift that no drawing room in London could have taught her.

At supper one evening Mr Hale announces, with ill-concealed pleasure, that Mr Thornton has asked to become his first pupil and will begin to attend as soon as his business allows. Late that night Margaret stands at her window and watches the lamps of the mills glow through the dark like lines of captive stars. She wonders, with idle curiosity, what sort of man a master of those great machines can be.

Mr Thornton arrives punctually for his first lesson, a tall, dark man of about thirty, with a strong, serious face and the stiff bearing of one who has always had to rely upon himself. He bows to Margaret without a trace of a smile, and she, her chin slightly raised, returns the courtesy with equal formality. Each of them, privately, thinks the other proud, and neither is entirely mistaken in that judgement.

He confesses, in his abrupt way, that his schooling ended too early and that he wishes to repair the loss by studying the great poets of Greece. Mr Hale, delighted to have so earnest a pupil, takes down the Iliad, and the two men bend their heads over the page. Mr Thornton reads each line with the stubborn determination of a man climbing a steep hill with a heavy load.

While Margaret pours the tea, the talk turns to the business of the town, and she remarks, with a little more scorn than she intended, that she cannot like anything that smells of the shop. Mr Thornton replies with perfect calm that the very cloth she is wearing was made by the labour of the north, and that there is nothing in trade to be ashamed of. He does not raise his voice, but she sees that she has wounded him.

Within a few weeks the lessons have grown into a friendship, and they often run on long beyond the hour as the two men argue happily over Homer and heroes. Margaret, sewing in the next room, overhears her father's laughter rising warmly through the wall, and she is quietly astonished by how much he enjoys it. She cannot quite decide whether to be grateful to Mr Thornton or jealous of him.

Not long afterwards Mrs Thornton herself comes to call at Crampton, a stern, upright woman with grey hair and a plain black dress, who bears the whole of her son's good name upon her shoulders. Her manners are perfect and her voice is level, yet her eyes travel over Margaret with the unhurried scrutiny of a merchant inspecting goods. Margaret feels herself judged and found, in some unspoken and wordless way, to be wanting in the qualities that matter.

A week later the Hales return the visit at Marlborough Mills, where the master and his family live in a stone house beside the very mill from which their fortune comes. Margaret pauses in the great yard and gazes up at the long, lighted building, which hums and shudders with a power she feels through the soles of her feet. It is the first time she has understood that the smoke, the noise and the crowds all begin here.

Mrs Thornton receives them in a parlour that is the very picture of cold propriety, with every chair under its cover and every ornament exactly where it was placed ten years before. As she speaks, and especially as she speaks of her son, it becomes plain that she sees in him the whole proof of her own life. Margaret respects the fierce devotion, even while she shrinks from the chill that surrounds it.

Fanny Thornton, the daughter of the house, is a pretty, restless girl in a fashionable dress, and she cannot resist asking Margaret a dozen eager questions about London and its shops. Margaret answers patiently, with a good deal of humour, and she is surprised to discover that she likes the girl rather better than she had expected. Mrs Thornton listens in silence, her mouth a little tight, as though she suspected her daughter of disloyalty.

As the visitors prepare to leave, Margaret glances out over the yard and sees Mr Thornton crossing it among his workers, a figure of quiet authority in his plain coat. The men touch their caps as he passes and drop their eyes, and she cannot tell whether it is respect or fear that she reads in their faces. She suspects, with a certain reluctant fairness, that what she is seeing is probably a mixture of both.

Walking home through the dim streets, Margaret announces that she does not like Mr Thornton and that she does not think she will ever learn to. Her father, who rarely contradicts her, shakes his head and says that the man is honest, sincere and brave, and that it would be wrong to judge him by his manner. She falls silent, still unconvinced, but a little ashamed of her haste and of the pleasure she took in disliking him.

On a walk through the poorer streets beyond Crampton, Margaret meets a pale, hollow-eyed girl who is leaning against a wall and coughing as though her chest would break. The girl lifts a worn face and says, with a tired smile, that her name is Bessy Higgins and that her sister Mary is waiting for her at home. Margaret, moved by something she cannot explain, offers to walk with her as far as the corner.

Bessy sinks down upon a doorstep to recover her breath and tells Margaret, without a trace of self-pity, that she works in the carding room of a mill, where the air is thick with fine white fluff. It fills her lungs like smoke, she says, and the doctor has told her she will not mend; she does not expect to live much longer. Margaret, who has never before heard death spoken of so quietly, finds that she has no words at all.

The next day Margaret asks leave to visit, and she climbs the narrow stairs of a cramped house to find a kitchen that is small and meagrely furnished but scrubbed to the very bone. A bright fire burns in the grate, a kettle sings upon it, and a little girl of about ten stands on a stool, stirring a pot. The poverty is plain, but so is the pride, and Margaret feels at once that she is a guest.

When Bessy's father comes in from the mill, he proves to be a broad, bearded man with a direct gaze, a rough voice and a ferocious dignity, and he greets the visitor with open suspicion. Nicholas Higgins tells her without apology that the masters care nothing for the men who serve them. A worker is valued only as long as his strength lasts, he says, and he for one has no wish to be thanked for his misery.

Higgins adds, with a hard look, that ladies generally come among the poor to preach and then go away, having done nothing but make themselves feel better. Margaret, who has been brought up never to be insolent and never to lie, answers that she has come only to see Bessy, and that she does not know enough about the matter to take either side. He studies her for a long moment, searching her face for any sign of pretence, and then, grudgingly, he nods.

On later visits Margaret reads to Bessy from a worn Bible that has been handled until its corners have softened, and the sick girl always asks for the last book, with its visions of a shining city. She loves its promise of a place where there shall be no more pain and no more crying, and her thin face grows peaceful as the words are read. Margaret, who had never fully understood the poetry of that book, discovers its meaning in her listener's longing.

One evening Mr Hale accompanies his daughter to the Higgins house, and he and Nicholas fall into a quiet conversation by the fire on faith, doubt and the difficulty of believing what one is told to believe. Higgins confesses that he has never been able to feel as his daughter does, and Mr Hale, who has suffered similar torments, listens with an understanding that no sermon could have conveyed. Margaret watches the two men talking so quietly together, and she loves her father more than she ever has before.

In the streets Margaret begins to notice little knots of men talking at the corners with lowered voices and a certain restless air, and Higgins explains to her that the workers have formed a Union. If the masters cut the wages, he says, the men will stop work together, and nothing will make them return until they have been heard. She hears in his voice both a threat and a plea, and she cannot tell which is the stronger.

At home, Mrs Hale grows steadily weaker, and Margaret sits up with her through the long nights, bathing her forehead and listening to her breathing. Dixon, who has been watching the daily excursions with growing disapproval, tells her sharply that a clergyman's daughter has no business spending her afternoons among mill families. Margaret answers quietly that she will go where she is needed, and that is the end of the argument.

One evening, when her mother is asleep and the house is still, Margaret stands at the window and looks out over the dark rooftops of Milton, studded with the red glow of furnaces. She realises that the masters and the workers inhabit two separate worlds in the same town, each ignorant of the other and each convinced of its own wrongs. She resolves, with the stubbornness she has inherited from her father, to try to understand them both.

One evening Mr Thornton lingers after his lesson and, in answer to a gentle question from Mr Hale, tells the story of his rise. His father died while he was a boy, leaving the family in debt and in disgrace, and at fifteen he had to leave school and take a place in a shop to keep his mother and sister from want. He relates it all in a plain, unboasting voice, as though describing the fortunes of a stranger.

He adds that for years he and his mother lived on almost nothing, counting every coin and sacrificing every comfort, until by slow degrees he had gathered enough to begin again for himself. Margaret, who has been sewing quietly in the corner, finds that her needle has stopped moving. She does not say a word, but something in her opinion of the man has shifted, like a stone settling in a stream.

A week later the Hales are invited to dine at Marlborough Mills, and since Mrs Hale is too ill to go, Margaret accompanies her father in a plain dress and a clean white collar. Dixon, fastening her mistress's daughter into the gown, tells her sternly to hold up her head among the northern ladies and to remember that she is a Hale of Helstone. Margaret smiles, though her heart is thumping a little, and she lifts her chin as she goes down the stairs.

The Thorntons' dining room is a blaze of silver, glass and polished mahogany, and the table is loaded with more dishes than any party could possibly finish. Mrs Thornton presides at the head of it like a queen at her coronation, and it is clear that every plate has been chosen to prove how far the family has risen. Margaret feels something very like admiration and something very like discomfort, and she cannot easily say which of them is stronger.

Over the wine the mill owners talk with the loud confidence of men who are rarely contradicted, and one of them, a Mr Hamper, declares that workers have no business to question their masters about wages, hours or anything else. A good hand, he says, does what he is told and goes quietly home, and the whole table murmurs its agreement. Mr Hale, who dislikes argument of every kind, studies his plate with the closest possible attention and does not lift his eyes.

Another master, a red-faced Mr Slickson, laughs and says that the hands are no more than great children, who must be kept in order or they will do themselves a mischief. Margaret, who has sat for hours by the bedside of a dying mill girl and drunk tea at the table of Nicholas Higgins, can scarcely keep her anger from showing in her face. She grips her napkin tightly in her lap until her knuckles whiten, and she bites back the words that are rising in her throat.

When the gentlemen join the ladies in the drawing room, she finds a quiet corner and speaks to Mr Thornton at last, in a low and trembling voice that is almost a challenge. She tells him honestly that she believes the masters of Milton to be far too hard on the people they employ, and that these workers have hearts and families and pride, just as the rich do. It is the boldest speech that she has ever made in her life, and she is startled to hear it in her own voice.

Mr Thornton listens with his hand resting heavily on the mantelpiece, and his answer, when it comes, is as measured as a verdict. A master who is not free to run his own mill as he sees fit, he says, cannot run it at all, and he has never taken a penny that he did not earn by his own labour. His eyes are hard, but there is a strange gleam in them that is not entirely anger.

Neither of them raises a voice, yet the cold politeness between them thickens with every sentence, until the air seems ready to crackle. Across the room, Mrs Thornton and Fanny watch closely, the mother with a tightening mouth and the daughter with wide, delighted eyes, and both can see how deeply the conversation has stirred their master. Margaret turns away first, her cheeks flushed and her thoughts uncertain, and she pretends to admire a vase on the table.

On the way home Margaret regrets some of her sharper words, though she cannot bring herself to take back any of her opinions, and she is silent for most of the walk. In his study at Marlborough Mills, Mr Thornton paces slowly up and down in the lamplight, thinking with surprising bitterness about a girl who has not once been afraid of him. He tells himself that he cares nothing for her good opinion, and he does not believe it.

Late one night Margaret sits alone by a guttering candle and reads, for the twentieth time, a worn letter from her brother Frederick, who lives in exile abroad. Nobody in Milton must hear that he exists, and she tucks the paper away among her father's manuscripts with a care that is almost superstitious. Secrets, she is beginning to find, weigh a great deal more heavily than any trunk that she has ever had to carry upstairs.

Frederick, a naval officer of great promise and a warmer heart than prudence, once joined a mutiny against a tyrannical captain, and for that crime he cannot set foot in England without risking the gallows. He has been absent for years from his parents and his sister, and his mother's one passionate dream is to see him again before she dies. Margaret feels the weight of that dream pressing upon every single day, like a stone she must carry in silence.

Mrs Hale grows steadily weaker, and at last Mr Hale sends for Dr Donaldson, a grave, gentle man who listens to her chest for a long time with a face that gives nothing away. In the passage afterwards he tells Margaret, in a low voice, that her mother is a good deal more ill than the family has been willing to admit. She thanks him in a steady voice, without letting him see how her hands are shaking, and then she goes upstairs to tell her father.

That season trade is poor, orders are slow and the cost of cotton is high, and the masters of Milton meet behind closed doors to decide what is to be done about wages. They agree, after long and heated talk, that they cannot afford any increase, and that any worker who objects is to be replaced without ceremony. In every mill owner's house across the town, the same cold resolution settles, and it is not softened by any thought of the families it will affect.

Higgins comes to the Hales' house with his cap crushed in his hands and tells Margaret that the Union has been holding meetings in the back rooms of the town. If the masters will not listen, he says, the men will stop work together, though it breaks his heart to think of the children who will go hungry. His voice is steady, but there is a strained look in his eyes that she has not seen before.

The next morning the workers stand in the street outside the mill gates with their tools laid down, and the great chimneys of Milton are quiet for the first time in Margaret's experience. The whole town seems to be holding its breath, waiting to learn whether the men or the masters will give way. The silence is stranger and more menacing than any noise could ever be, and it hangs over every street.

In the poorest streets, where no one had savings to begin with, food begins to run short, and neighbours share what they can with neighbours who have less. A thin, nervous man named Boucher stands in his doorway with half a dozen hollow-cheeked children behind him, and his wife sits inside too weary to speak. Margaret leaves what she has in her basket and feels it to be an insult.

Mr Thornton will not bend, and he declares through his teeth that he will not be dictated to by his own hands, whatever the cost to his profits. He sends secretly to Ireland for labourers who will accept the wages he offers, and he confides his plan to nobody except his mother and his foreman. In the quiet of Marlborough Mills he sits in his office with a face like stone.

Rumours of the plan reach Margaret, and in alarm she goes straight to Mr Thornton to beg him to think of the fury it must cause among men already driven half mad by hunger. He listens courteously, as he always does, and then answers shortly that it is the only way to keep his mill alive and that he has no choice in the matter. She leaves with the bitter sense that two honest wills are marching toward a collision.

Boucher goes from group to group among the idle men, and his speeches grow wilder as his children's faces grow thinner, until his hatred of the Irish seems to have swallowed his own grief. Higgins, hearing him on the canal bank at dusk, shakes his head and mutters a warning, for he knows better than anyone how quickly a hungry crowd may turn to violence. The night closes in on the town, and in house after house nobody sleeps well, for everyone senses that tomorrow will bring something terrible.

At dawn the Irish labourers arrive at Marlborough Mills in a tight, silent column, hemmed in by guards, with hats pulled low over their eyes. The strikers watch from the opposite pavement, grim and motionless, and a murmur like the growl of an animal passes along their ranks as the gates swing shut. Nobody speaks a word, but every man in the street understands that a line has been crossed and that it cannot be uncrossed.

By midday the crowd outside the mill has swollen to several hundred, and the shouting at the gate has taken on a dangerous, rhythmic edge. Higgins pushes his way among the men, pleading with them in a hoarse voice to go home before it is too late, but nobody will listen to a man who is not as angry as they are. His words are swallowed by the clamour as if they had never been spoken.

Margaret has come with a message for the Thorntons and has no notion of what awaits her until she turns the corner and finds the street choked with workers. She pushes through a gap in the crowd, slips in at the gates just before they are closed, and discovers that she has walked into the middle of a siege. Behind her, as the heavy gates swing shut, the din of the crowd rises like a tide against a wall.

Suddenly the mob begins to throw stones, and the ground-floor windows of the house shatter one after another with a sound like breaking ice. Mrs Thornton orders the servants to take a frightened Fanny to the back rooms, and a messenger is sent running for the soldiers, though nobody can say how long they will take. The whole house fills with dust and glitter and the smell of fear, and every face is white in the half-light.

Margaret finds Mr Thornton standing at an upper window, looking down at the sea of angry faces with the expression of a man resolved to endure it, and she implores him to go out and speak to the people. If he does not, she says, the soldiers will fire upon starving men, and the blood will be upon his conscience for the rest of his life. He turns on her a long gaze full of pride and doubt, and she does not look away from it.

For a moment he says nothing, and then, as if some invisible lever has been pulled, he pushes open the door and steps out alone into the roaring daylight. Margaret does not stop to think but follows him at once, because she cannot bear to let him face that crowd without her. The noise breaks over the two of them like a wave over a rock.

A man at the front of the crowd lifts a heavy stone, and without a thought for herself Margaret throws her arms around Mr Thornton's shoulders to shield him with her own body. The stone strikes her on the forehead, and she sinks against his chest as the blood runs warm down her cheek, and the whole world narrows to a single ringing note. Through the ringing in her ears, she hears him cry out her name, as if from the other end of a long tunnel.

Mr Thornton holds her up, and the crowd, which a moment earlier was howling for his blood, falls suddenly and strangely silent at the sight of a woman hurt. Men who were shouting a moment ago now stare at the pavement, ashamed, and some of them turn quietly away, as though each were afraid of meeting another's eyes. The fury has gone out of them all at once, like air from a bellows, and nothing remains but a heavy, shamed quiet.

Within minutes the soldiers come marching into the yard in their red coats, with a clatter of boots and a ringing of orders, and the crowd melts away before them down the side streets. By the time the first rank reaches the gate there is scarcely anyone left to arrest, and the great yard lies empty in the pale light. The siege is over almost as suddenly as it began, and the silence that follows seems louder than the shouting.

Mr Thornton carries Margaret into the parlour, where Mrs Thornton and Fanny bathe the wound and bind it with linen. The old lady performs her duty with an expressionless face, but there is a hard, watchful look in her eyes, for she has seen the way her son looked at the girl and she knows what it means. Margaret, half conscious on the sofa, notices that the old lady says nothing at all, and the silence is more eloquent than words.

Margaret is carried home with her forehead bound in linen, pale and a little dazed, and her father turns white when he hears from the servant what she has done. She tells him calmly that she would have done the same for any man, and he is too much moved to answer, for he is only now beginning to understand how brave and impulsive his daughter has grown. He sits beside her sofa all through the long afternoon, holding her hand, until at last she falls into a heavy sleep.

The next morning Mr Thornton calls at the Hales' door with his hat in his hand and asks, in a voice that he can hardly control, whether Miss Hale is well enough to see him. He has not slept, and his face is grey and drawn, but his eyes are bright with a purpose he does not trouble to hide. Mr Hale, who guesses nothing, shows him into the little parlour and leaves the two of them alone.

With none of the polish he displays at his own table, Mr Thornton tells Margaret in a low, rough voice that he loves her and wishes her to be his wife. He has loved her, he says, almost since the first day he saw her, and neither her scorn nor her silence has been able to alter it. His hands, as he speaks, are clenched at his sides, and she can see that the words cost him more than any battle in the mill yard.

Margaret has long considered him a proud, hard man, and she cannot believe that he speaks from anything but a sense of honour, since she was hurt in his defence. She answers coldly, saying that she does not want his gratitude, that she would have acted so for any man in danger, and that she has no wish to be his wife. Every word lands upon him like a blow, though she is too proud to see it.

Mr Thornton bows, tells her quietly that she has mistaken him, and leaves the room without another syllable, closing the door as softly as if the house were full of sleepers. Margaret remains at the window for a long time, trembling from head to foot, and she tells herself again and again that she feels nothing at all. The more often she says it, the less she believes it, and by evening she has stopped saying it altogether.

When Mrs Thornton hears of the refusal, her face turns to granite, for she can hardly believe that a girl with no fortune and very little standing would reject a man like her son. Fanny, listening, hides a secret smile behind her sewing, and the whole house falls under a silence so heavy that even the servants walk on tiptoe. The old lady's pride, wounded so deeply on her son's behalf, is not the kind that forgives easily or forgets at all.

In the poor streets the strike is breaking, for the little savings have gone, the pawnshops are full and the children are crying with hunger in every doorway. Day by day, more of the men creep back to the mill gates with their caps in their hands, ashamed to ask for work but too hungry to stay away. The great stand of the Union is wearing out like a rope that has been strained too long.

Margaret goes to see Higgins, who is sitting by a cold fireplace in a house stripped of almost everything of value, stubborn and silent, like a man holding up a wall. His daughter is ill upstairs and the larder is empty, yet he declares in a flat voice that he would sooner starve than go back and say that the masters were right. She sees that it is pride and love, not folly, that keeps him there.

At last the strike collapses altogether, and the men file back through the mill gates with bowed heads, accepting the wages they had refused and the terms they had fought. The masters have won, but the victory has an ashen taste, for many families are poorer and angrier than they were before, and the men who led the Union are quietly marked. Nothing between masters and men has really been settled, because the whole quarrel has only been postponed for a while.

That night Margaret stands alone at her window while the lamps of Milton burn red in the smoke, and she wishes with all her heart that she had spoken more gently to Mr Thornton. She cannot say why his face keeps returning to her, with its look of stunned and silent pain, and she does not dare to look too closely for the answer. Somewhere in the dark, she thinks, there are two people who have misjudged each other.

Bessy grows weaker with every day, and Margaret sits beside her narrow bed for hours at a time, watching the thin chest rise and fall with the labour of each breath. Mary has gone to work at the mill, and the little house is so quiet that she can hear the fire settling in the grate. It is a silence that she will remember vividly for the rest of her life, long after the room itself has been forgotten.

Bessy turns her face upon the worn pillow and speaks gently of her short life, of the mill and the long hours and the troubles of the town that has used her up. She thanks Margaret for her friendship, and says that she has never had such a friend before, and that she would not have missed knowing her for anything. Margaret, unable to find any answer that would be good enough, simply presses her thin hand and lets the silence speak for her.

As the evening light spreads across the room, Bessy asks her to read once more from the last book of the Bible, the one with the shining city and the river of life. Margaret reads slowly, in a voice that wavers on the hardest verses, and Bessy's lips move silently with the familiar words as though they were a prayer she had known since childhood. Outside the window, far away across the roofs, the factory whistles blow for the night and the town begins to grow quiet.

Bessy holds Margaret's hand with surprising strength and whispers that her father will be left alone and does not know how to be comforted. She begs Margaret to be kind to him, for he is proud and quick to anger, but there is a good heart under all his roughness and he has never had an easy life. Margaret promises that she will, and she means it with the whole of her soul, though she has no idea how it will be done.

A single candle burns beside the bed as the shadows lengthen across the walls, and Bessy lies very still with her eyes half closed. At dusk her breathing slows, hesitates and then stops altogether, so gently that Margaret does not understand for a moment what has happened. Then she lowers her head onto the quilt, and the tears she has been holding back fall at last.

Higgins comes in from the street and stands in the doorway of the small kitchen, his cap in his hand, looking across at the bed where his daughter lies. For a long moment he says nothing at all, and then he sits down heavily by the fire and covers his face with his rough hands. Margaret has never seen a strong man so broken, and she cannot find a single word that would help.

Margaret stays until Mary comes home from her work, and then she walks back to Crampton through streets that are dark and wet with rain, the lamps wavering in the puddles. She thinks of the girl who was a stranger only a few months ago and who has taught her more about courage than any book, and she thinks of the father who is left behind with nothing but his pride. By the time she reaches her own front door the tears are running unchecked down her face, and she does not trouble to wipe them away.

At home Mrs Hale has grown weaker still, and she lies back on her pillows and looks at her daughter with an expression of such deep longing that Margaret can hardly bear it. She tells her, in a thin and trembling voice, that she wants more than anything in the world to see her son Frederick once more before she dies. It is the first time in many months that she has spoken of him aloud, and the name seems to fill the whole room like a bell.

Mr Hale and Dixon talk anxiously in the dim hallway, because they both know the terrible danger that waits for Frederick if he ever sets foot in England, with a price still hanging over his name. Mrs Hale cries and begs and clings to her husband's sleeve, and in the end nobody in the house has the heart to say no to a dying woman. In this way, without a word ever being spoken between them, the decision is made, and it can no longer be undone by anyone.

Margaret sits down at her desk and writes a letter to her brother, choosing every word with great care, while her mother lies sleeping at last in the next room. She knows perfectly well that if the letter is intercepted, or if Frederick is recognised in the street, he may be arrested and condemned, and that the blame will be hers. She seals it at last and addresses it with a hand that is not quite steady, and then she sits for a long time without moving.

Margaret waits day after day at the window, running to the door each time the postman knocks, until she is certain that the letter has been lost or intercepted. At last, on a grey morning, a thin envelope arrives in an unfamiliar foreign hand, and she reads it with trembling fingers: Frederick will come as soon as he can arrange his passage. She cries a little from sheer relief, and then she goes to tell Dixon.

Mr Hale and Dixon prepare a quiet room at the back of the house, and the whole family agrees, in whispers, to tell nobody in Milton. Dixon scrubs the floor and hangs a dark curtain across the window, muttering that she would guard Master Frederick with her very life, and none of the three doubts her. The little house settles into a strange, hushed sort of expectancy, like a theatre in the moment before the curtain goes up.

One dark night there comes a soft knock at the door, and a tall, sunburnt young man steps in, wrapped in a heavy travelling coat and carrying a battered bag. Margaret throws her arms around him with a cry that she muffles in his shoulder, and for a moment neither of them is able to speak at all. He smells of the sea and the road, and she thinks that she has never loved anyone so much.

Frederick goes upstairs without waiting to take off his coat, and he kneels beside his mother's bed, saying her name over and over in a low voice. Mrs Hale lifts both her thin hands and touches his face as if she could hardly believe that he was real, and her eyes fill with the tears of a happiness she has waited so many years to feel. The whole room seems lit from within, and for a little while even the lamp looks brighter than it did before.

Later Frederick sits with his father and sister beside a small lamp and tells them the whole of his story, speaking quietly and without self-pity. The captain of his ship, the Orion, had been so cruel that the sailors rose against him, he explains, and although he himself had tried to calm the men, he had been judged as guilty as any of them. Margaret hears it with a heavy heart, for she can see that he has paid a great price for a single hot-headed moment.

For a few days the house is happier than it has been since the family left Helstone, and Mrs Hale seems so much better that Mr Hale begins, in his gentle way, to hope. Frederick and Margaret laugh together at supper over some old joke from their childhood, and the old servant, hearing them from the kitchen, cannot help smiling into her apron. It is a brief, bright interval, and they all sense that it cannot last.

Dixon peers anxiously through the curtains at the street whenever she passes the window, afraid that a neighbour or a stranger will recognise the visitor and carry the tale to someone with a reason to remember. Margaret reminds her brother again and again that he must keep away from the glass and never go out by daylight, and he promises with a rueful laugh to be careful. Even so, she cannot rid herself of a growing dread that she is unable to explain, and it follows her from room to room.

On the fourth day Mrs Hale grows suddenly weaker, and in a great hurry Dr Donaldson is sent for, arriving with his bag and his grave, kindly face. He examines her gently and then draws Margaret out into the hall, where he tells her in a low voice that there is nothing more to be done and that the end cannot be far off. She nods, because she has known it for some time, and goes back into the room.

Mrs Hale takes her children's hands, one on each side of the bed, and speaks to them tenderly and quite clearly, as though the illness had lifted for an hour. She asks them to look after their father, who is helpless without her, and to be kind to each other whatever may happen, and she says in a soft voice that she is happy at last. Neither of them is able to answer her, for the tears are running down both their faces, and they can only hold her hands more tightly.

The clock ticks steadily in the silent room as the family gathers around the bed, and nobody has the heart to leave, although the fire has sunk low and the lamp needs trimming. Mrs Hale falls into a deep, quiet sleep, and Margaret and Frederick sit holding her hands through the long hours of the night, listening to her slow breathing. Outside the window, the town is silent for once, as if it too were waiting.

At dawn, as the grey light creeps across the floor, Mrs Hale dies peacefully with her son and daughter holding her hands, and there is nothing in her face but rest. Margaret bends and kisses her mother's forehead, and Frederick remains on his knees beside the bed long after there is no further need. Nobody speaks, and the clock in the hall goes on ticking as though nothing had changed.

Mr Hale is crushed by grief and can hardly speak, and he clings to Margaret's arm as they lay his wife to rest in a quiet corner of the Milton cemetery, under a sky that is the colour of ashes. Frederick, who cannot risk being seen, watches from a distance among the trees, and he is the last to turn away. It is a small, silent funeral, and to Margaret, who remembers the church bells and flowers of Helstone, it seems almost cruelly plain.

That same evening Frederick tells his sister that he must leave before anybody grows suspicious, and Margaret, who cannot bear the thought of his going alone, insists on seeing him to the station. Dixon begs her not to go out, warning her of what the neighbours will say, but Margaret is deaf to all arguments. She puts on her bonnet and shawl without another word, and she takes her place at her brother's side in the doorway.

The brother and sister walk arm in arm through the dark streets, passing beneath the gas lamps that hiss and flicker above them, and they try to look like any ordinary young couple on an errand. Margaret holds his sleeve so tightly that her fingers ache, and neither of them speaks, for each knows that a single wrong word might be heard by a passing stranger. The whole town, with its shuttered windows and its dark doorways, seems to lean in and listen to their footsteps.

On the platform they stand close together in the shadows, saying their farewells in low, hurried voices, and Margaret does not see that Mr Thornton is passing nearby on his way home from a meeting. He sees Margaret with a young man whom he does not know, holding her arm with an air of intimacy, and he walks on with a cold, sick feeling spreading through his heart. In that moment the worst possible explanation seems to him the only one, and he does not stay to look any closer.

Just as the train is about to leave, a shabby man standing beneath one of the lamps stares hard at Frederick's face and takes a step closer. His name is Leonards, and he once knew the family in happier days, and he announces in a loud, triumphant voice that he knows exactly who this young man is. Margaret feels the blood drain from her face, and she cannot find any voice with which to protest or deny it.

Leonards seizes Frederick by the arm, and in an instant there is a violent struggle at the very edge of the platform, with shouts and the scuffle of boots. Frederick, fighting for his life, pushes the man away with all his strength, and he falls heavily to the ground and lies where he has fallen. For one terrible second nobody on the whole platform moves or speaks, and even the engine seems to hold its breath.

Frederick looks back once at his sister, with a face full of love and horror, and then leaps onto the moving train as the carriage doors swing shut behind him. Margaret watches the red lamp at the back of the last carriage dwindle into the darkness, and she feels her knees begin to shake beneath her. She cannot tell, as she stands there in the steam and the dark, whether she has just saved her brother or lost him for ever.

Leonards lies on the stones groaning, and a small crowd gathers around him with exclamations and questions, so that for a few moments nobody is paying any attention to the pale young woman at the edge of the lamplight. Margaret, who is shaking from head to foot, steps back into the shadows and slips away before anyone thinks to ask her who she is. She does not look behind her once, for she is afraid that if she does, she will lose all of her courage.

She walks home alone through the dark town with her heart pounding in her ears and climbs the stairs of the silent house, where her father is asleep at last in the room below. Alone in her room, with the door shut, she bursts into tears, afraid for her brother, afraid for the man who fell and afraid of what the morning may bring. Too frightened to lie down, she sits on the edge of the bed with her hands clasped in her lap until the first light creeps in.

The next morning a police inspector knocks at the Hales' door with his hat in his hand and a look of professional gravity on his face. He tells Margaret that the man who fell at the station has died of his injuries, and he adds that the matter is more serious than anyone supposed, because a young woman was seen with the man who pushed him. Margaret receives the news with a face carved from marble and a heart that has turned to ice.

The inspector takes a chair in the parlour and opens a small notebook upon his knee, while Margaret stands before him with her hands folded and her heart beating so loudly that she is certain he must hear it. He asks her, politely but very directly, whether she was at the railway station on the previous evening, and he waits with his pencil poised above the page. The clock on the mantelpiece ticks away one long, slow second after another, and the whole room seems to wait.

For a moment the room is perfectly still, and then Margaret lifts her chin and answers in a clear voice that she was at home all the evening. It is the first lie of her whole life, and it seems to burn her tongue like a coal as she speaks. Yet she delivers it without a tremor, for her brother's life is the price of any hesitation.

The inspector looks at her with kindly eyes, closes his notebook with a snap and thanks her for her time, apologising for the intrusion upon a house of mourning. When the door has shut behind him, Margaret has to hold on to the back of a chair, for her knees are trembling so badly that she can hardly stand upright. She has saved Frederick, she thinks, but in doing it she has lost something in herself that she is afraid she will never find again.

At his magistrate's desk, Mr Thornton receives the inspector's report and learns that a young woman answering exactly to Margaret's description was seen at the station, and that Miss Hale has denied it. He understands at once that she has lied, and his face does not move, but he thinks of the young man at her side and of the tenderness of the way she held his arm. He lets the matter drop without a word, but the worse opinion he forms of her that day is a hard thing for him to bear.

Margaret sits alone in a darkened room with her hand pressed over her eyes, deeply ashamed that she has lied and that no one but herself can ever know why. She cannot understand why Mr Thornton has been so cold to her in the past few days, and she does not guess how much he has seen or what he has made of it. The grief for her mother and the guilt for her lie press upon her together, and in the darkness she cannot separate the one from the other.

A few days later some men find the body of Boucher in a shallow stream beside an old stone bridge, and the news runs through the town in an hour. He had lost his place at the mills after the strike and had gone hungry for weeks, and nobody can say how he came to be in the water, though everyone knows how desperate he had grown. His wife, who is already ill, is left alone with six hungry children and no money in the house to feed them.

Higgins, who never liked the man and quarrelled with him bitterly in the weeks of the strike, nevertheless takes in Boucher's three smallest children, saying gruffly that he cannot let them starve. He leads them home through the narrow streets of the town, a hand held in each of his, and Mary follows behind with a bundle, saying nothing against it. Margaret, who sees them pass from the corner of the street, feels her eyes sting, and she remembers the promise she made to Bessy.

Because he was a leader of the Union, the masters of Milton have closed their gates against him, and Higgins's house is almost bare of food and of hope. He sits at the table in his kitchen and counts a few coins in his palm, over and over again, as if the number might change, and he knows that they cannot last the week. The children eat whatever he gives them, and he himself, for several days now, has eaten almost nothing at all.

At last Higgins swallows his pride, puts on his cleanest jacket and walks to Marlborough Mills, and he stands outside the great gates with his cap crushed in his hand. He has never in his life asked a master for a favour, and every line of his body seems to say that he hates to do so now, yet the children at home give him no choice. The porter looks him up and down with an unfriendly eye, and then, after a long pause, he goes across the yard to find the master.

Mr Thornton comes out to the gate and looks hard at Higgins, who tells him plainly that he was a leader of the Union and does not regret it. He asks only for work, he says, and he will do it honestly, for he has children to feed and no more pride than he can afford. Thornton, who respects plain speaking above every other quality, studies him for a long moment and tells him to start in the morning.

Later in the week the two men sit together at a bare wooden table in the mill office and talk openly, for the first time in their lives, as one man to another. Higgins describes how the strike looked from below, with its hunger and its dark rooms and its fear, and Thornton listens without interrupting and without any of his usual anger. It is a conversation that neither of them would have thought possible a month before.

Thornton is struck by what he has heard, and he decides to open a cheap dining room at the mill where his workers may have a hot, plain meal at a fair price. It is a small step, hardly more than a gesture, but it begins to melt the old mistrust between the master and his men, who have never before been given anything by the man they work for. Higgins is the first to eat there, and the first to say that the soup is good.

Higgins calls at the Hales' house to tell Margaret that he has found work at Marlborough Mills, and he stands awkwardly in the parlour turning his cap in his hands. She is delighted, and she says warmly that she always knew there was good in Mr Thornton, even if he took pains to hide it. Higgins, with a ghost of a smile, answers that the master may have more of a heart than he lets on.

Not long afterwards Mr Bell arrives in Milton, a small, brisk old gentleman in black clothes, who greets Mr Hale like a brother and looks him up and down with a frown of concern. He sees at once how tired and thin his friend has grown since his wife's death, and he declares, in his usual abrupt manner, that Mr Hale must come to Oxford for a rest and will accept no refusal. Margaret, listening from the doorway, silently blesses him, and she is more grateful than she knows how to say.

Mr Hale hesitates, since he does not like to leave his daughter alone in the house so soon after her mother's death, but she tells him, smiling, that the change will do him good. She packs his small bag with her own hands, straightens his coat and kisses him goodbye at the door, and she stands on the step to wave until the cab has turned the corner. She does not know, as she turns back into the quiet house, that she will never see him again in this world.

In Oxford Mr Hale walks beneath the old trees of the college gardens beside his friend, among the grey stone walls and the quiet courts where he spent his youth, and he feels almost young again. He meets old companions in the common room and talks for hours about books and poets and the long-ago days, and for the first time in many months he is truly and simply happy. Mr Bell, watching him from across the table, thinks that the whole long journey has been worth it for this alone.

On the last afternoon Mr Hale sits quietly in a garden chair as the light fades from gold to grey, and he seems to be dozing over the book that lies open on his knee. When Mr Bell comes to wake him for tea, he finds that his old friend has died peacefully in his sleep, with a smile still upon his face. Somewhere above the old roofs the college bell strikes the hour, and the garden below it is very still.

A message brings the news to Margaret, and she travels to Oxford at once, with a face so white and fixed that the people on the train look away from her out of delicacy. She stands in her dark dress outside the college gate, and for a long moment she cannot bring herself to go in, because to cross the threshold is to make it true. Then she lifts her head, straightens her black dress, and walks slowly through the gate as her father would have wished.

Margaret sits at a window in Mr Bell's rooms while he talks gently beside her, and he tells her, with an old man's clumsy tenderness, that she must not stay alone in Milton. She has lost both her parents within a few short months, and she is too stunned to argue, so she lets him persuade her to go and live with her aunt in London. Behind the glass, the quiet courts lie green and still in the evening light, and she cannot imagine ever leaving them.

Margaret arrives at the house in Harley Street dressed from head to foot in black, and Aunt Shaw hurries into the hall to gather her in her arms, with tears running down her powdered cheeks. She says that Margaret must now think of this house as her true and lasting home, and that nothing shall be wanting to her comfort. Margaret, who feels as though she were walking in a dream, thanks her in a low voice.

She is given a pretty room of her own that looks out over the quiet street, with a soft carpet and a bed hung with pale curtains, yet she feels numb and curiously far away. She puts away her few possessions in the unfamiliar drawers, and then she sits for a long while with her hands lying idle in her lap. She cannot decide what she ought to do next, and nobody comes to tell her.

Edith has returned from Corfu with a small baby, and she lies upon the sofa, as she always did, talking contentedly of the voyage and the heat. The child sleeps in the crook of her arm while she describes the doings of the regiment at great length. Margaret listens in silence, truly glad that her cousin is happy, but she cannot find it in herself to join in the talk.

Every evening there are visitors, and Margaret sits in the drawing room among the lamps and the flowers, hearing the same polite conversation about fashion, health and the prospects of the season. After the hard truths and the sorrows of Milton, it all seems small and hollow, like a play performed upon a stage where nobody is allowed to say what he means. She smiles at the right moments and thinks of something else entirely, and nobody seems to notice the difference.

One wet afternoon Margaret stands at the drawing-room window and watches the rain stream down the glass and gather in the gutters of the square below. She finds herself thinking, with a force that surprises her, of Higgins and Bessy, of the harsh bell of the mill and the smoky, crowded, vigorous streets of the north that she once found so ugly. It is a longing of a kind that she did not expect to feel.

Henry Lennox comes to dinner one evening, grown a little graver and a little more successful, and he treats Margaret with perfect kindness and not the slightest hint of resentment. They talk easily across the table, like old friends who have agreed to forget something, and she is grateful beyond words that her refusal has not spoiled his good opinion. Mrs Shaw watches them both across the table with an interested and rather hopeful eye, as though she had begun to make plans of her own.

Alone one afternoon in the park, beneath the dripping trees, Margaret turns over in her mind everything she knows about Mr Thornton, his pride and his courage and the way he spoke of his mother. She remembers his proposal and her cold answer, and for the first time she wonders honestly whether she may have misjudged him. Perhaps, she thinks, her own pride was as great as his, and perhaps it was far less excusable.

One evening Henry shows her a newspaper folded back at a column about the state of trade, and he remarks in a casual voice that the cotton business has suffered a particularly hard year. Several of the mills in the north are in serious trouble, he adds, and some of the oldest firms are said to be tottering, and Margaret feels a quick stab of fear that she cannot account for. She asks him to tell her more, but he does not know any names.

In Milton, at the same hour, Mr Thornton works late into the night at his account books, hunched over the figures with a single candle burning low beside him and the great mill silent in the dark beyond the window. Orders have fallen, debts have grown, and there is hardly a day on which some new difficulty does not arrive by the post. He does everything in his power to keep the business alive, and he tells nobody how afraid he is.

One morning at breakfast a letter arrives from Mr Bell, who writes in his abrupt style that he plans to visit Helstone and would like Margaret to go with him, since he is old and dislikes travelling alone. She accepts at once, her face glowing for the first time since her father's death. She knows well that the visit will be as painful as it is sweet, and she hurries upstairs to begin her packing without delay.

Margaret and Mr Bell travel south together, first by train and then by a hired carriage that rattles over the narrow roads, and she grows more eager with every mile as the familiar landmarks begin to appear. The lanes are green, the hedges are loud with birds, and she feels, for the first time in many months, almost like a girl again. Mr Bell, wrapped in his coat, watches her with quiet satisfaction, and he does not say a word to spoil her happiness.

At Helstone she stands beneath the great oak on the common and looks around the village, but she soon finds that much is different from the picture she has carried in her heart. New people live in the vicarage, the garden has been rearranged by strange hands, and the roses she once loved have been cut back. She feels like a visitor in a house that she once owned, and she turns away before the tears can come.

She walks through the village and calls upon the cottagers, and some of them weep with joy when they see her, but many of the old faces are gone, and those that remain are older and slower than she remembered. Even the lanes that seemed so wide and golden in her memory look narrow and quiet now, and the forest seems smaller. She understands, with a sad kind of wisdom, that it is she who has changed and not the place, and that she can never go back.

Mr Bell, tired out by the journey and the excitement of the visit, becomes so ill one evening that he must be put to bed at the village inn, and the local doctor is summoned in great haste. Margaret nurses him for several days with the same patient devotion she gave her mother, and she is glad to be of use to one who has been so kind to her family. Slowly he mends, though he never regains his colour, and she cannot help watching him with growing anxiety.

As he lies back on a heap of pillows, Mr Bell speaks quietly of his old friend Mr Hale, and of their youth together at Oxford, when they thought they could change the world. He says gruffly that he wants to see Margaret provided for, and she is touched, though she hardly attends to his words, for she is thinking of the doctor's frowning face in the passage. It will be some weeks before she understands what he meant, and by then it will be too late to thank him.

As soon as Mr Bell is strong enough to travel, a carriage takes him back to Oxford, and Margaret stands waving at the inn door until the road bends. She returns herself to Harley Street the next day, but she cannot shake off the feeling that the old man has not truly recovered. His last look at her, from the window of the carriage, stays in her mind for a long time afterwards, and she cannot say why it troubles her.

Some weeks afterwards a letter with a black border arrives in the drawing room in Harley Street, and Margaret reads, with a sinking heart, that Mr Bell has died at Oxford. She sits quite still with the paper in her hand, remembering the gruff, kindly old gentleman who had been her father's friend for forty years and her own in the short time she had known him. Once again the world seems a little emptier and a little colder, as it does each time a person she loves is taken away.

After the funeral a lawyer reads the will aloud to Margaret in a quiet, dusty room, and she listens at first with the polite blankness of a mourner. To her astonishment, Mr Bell has left her the whole of his fortune, including the buildings and grounds of Marlborough Mills in Milton, so that she is suddenly a woman of considerable wealth. She asks him twice whether he has read the paper correctly, and twice he assures her, with a smile, that he has.

Henry Lennox, who is well versed in such matters, becomes Margaret's adviser, and he explains the papers to her patiently across a polished table, with his usual cleverness and good humour. He tells her that the buildings of Marlborough Mills are rented by a Mr Thornton, a manufacturer of some standing, so that the man whose proposal she once refused is now, unknown to himself, her tenant. She is silent for a long moment, and when she looks up, her face has a new and thoughtful expression that he cannot read.

A few days later, in the course of business, Henry remarks that he has heard some disquieting news from the north, for Mr Thornton's mill is said to be in serious difficulties. Margaret, who has been sitting very straight, asks him anxiously what can be done, and he promises, with a puzzled glance at her pale face, to find out everything that he can. She hardly sleeps at all that night, and she lies awake in the dark until the clock on the stairs has struck every hour.

A great order fails at the worst possible moment, and the figures in the ledger on Mr Thornton's desk show beyond argument that he cannot pay what he owes. For weeks he has tried every means he knows to save the mill, selling, borrowing and bargaining, but in the end there is nothing left to try. He closes the book at last with a hand that does not shake, though he feels that something inside him has broken.

One morning Mr Thornton calls his workers together in the yard of Marlborough Mills and tells them plainly that he can no longer pay their wages and that the mill must close. They hear him in silence, and then they file out through the gates with their heads bowed, the same gates through which they once surged in anger. The heavy bar is dropped behind them for the last time, and the sound echoes across the empty yard.

Higgins stands alone in the empty yard and looks back at the closed gate, as the grey afternoon light falls on the silent windows of the mill. He is sorry, very sorry, for the master who gave him a chance when no other would, and he wonders what will happen to the town without the man who, for all his hardness, had learned to listen. It is a feeling that he would never have thought to expect, and he stands there a long time before he turns and goes.

Mrs Thornton sits bolt upright in her stiff parlour while the servants cover the furniture with cloths, and she does not complain, or weep, or reproach anyone. She says only, in her level voice, that she has faced hard times before and can face them again, and that she is proud of her son whatever happens. Only the tight grip of her hands in her lap, and the whiteness of her knuckles, shows anyone what the words are costing her.

Mr Thornton travels to London in the hope of finding help, and among his errands is a call upon a lawyer named Henry Lennox, who has some business concerning the property of the mill. He waits in the outer office with his hat on his knee, sitting very straight and looking at nothing. He has no idea whom he is about to meet, or what he is about to be told.

Henry looks up from his desk with a smile of polite surprise, and in the course of conversation he mentions that Miss Margaret Hale is the owner of Marlborough Mills, having inherited the buildings from Mr Bell. Thornton stares at him, amazed to learn that the girl who refused him is now his landlady, and for a moment he can find nothing at all to say. Then he laughs once, without any mirth, and asks Henry to go on, since there may be more to hear.

After a long pause Thornton asks, with an effort at carelessness, about a young man he once saw with Miss Hale at the railway station on a night in the autumn. Henry replies, with a smile of recollection, that it must have been Margaret's brother Frederick, a sailor in exile, who came to England in secret when their mother lay dying, as Mr Bell once told him in confidence. The room seems to spin around the listener, and the walls seem to lean in upon him from every side.

Mr Thornton leaves the office like a man in a dream and walks for a long time along the crowded London streets, seeing nothing, hearing nothing and thinking only of the lie he heard in the magistrate's room. He sees at last that he has misjudged her cruelly, that she lied not for love but for loyalty, and a bitter, burning regret rises in him like a tide. By the time the lamps are lit along the streets, he has quite made up his mind about what he must do.

On an impulse, Mr Thornton goes to the house in Harley Street, and he is shown into the drawing room, where Margaret rises from the sofa in surprise with a book still in her hand. They greet each other with formal courtesy, and for a moment neither of them knows where to look, for each has been thinking of the other far more than either would be willing to admit. The clock on the mantelpiece ticks loudly in the long, awkward pause that follows, and neither of them is willing to be the first to break it.

Mr Thornton tells Margaret that he must leave Milton, for there is nothing left there for him, and he thanks her for her kindness to Higgins and his family. He bows, with the stiff dignity that she remembers so well, and says that he must go. He does not seem to want to move, however, and she cannot find any words with which to detain him.

Margaret takes a folded paper from her bag and holds it out across the table with a hand that trembles only a little. In a low, clear voice she tells Mr Thornton that she wishes to lend him a sum from her fortune, enough to pay his creditors and to set the mill running again. He looks at the paper for a long while, but he does not reach out to take it.

Mr Thornton stands stiffly with his hands clasped behind his back, his face as unmoved as a carved stone, and says that he cannot accept so generous an offer from her or from anyone. His pride, which has carried him through poverty, strikes and ruin, is as strong as ever, and he cannot bear the thought of owing so much to the woman he loves. His refusal, though perfectly polite, sounds very much like the final word, and she feels her hope begin to fail.

Margaret leans forward earnestly and says that it is not charity but a plain business arrangement between a landlady and her tenant, and that she expects to be repaid with interest. She reminds him that the mill is her property, that its silence is costing her money as well as his, and that Higgins and a hundred other men are waiting for the gates to open again. Her voice does not waver once as she speaks, and her eyes never leave his face.

For a long moment Mr Thornton looks away, out of the window toward the grey roofs and the smoking chimneys of a city that is not his own, and she sees the struggle in his face. Then he turns back to her with a smile that she has never seen before, which softens every line of his hard features. He says that he will accept her offer, and that he will repay every penny of it, with thanks that he cannot yet put into words.

They sit together in the lamplight and speak honestly at last, of the night at the station, of Margaret's lie and of the dreadful conclusion that he drew from it. Each begs the other's pardon, and they discover with something between laughter and tears that they have both been proud, both been blind and both been utterly wrong. A great weight seems to fall from the room, and the air feels lighter than it has for a year.

Mr Thornton rises, comes slowly to stand close beside Margaret, and asks her in a voice so low that she can hardly hear it whether she could ever learn to love him. She says nothing, but she lifts her eyes to his and smiles, and the smile is a more eloquent answer than any speech. He draws a long breath, and his heart seems to beat in the silence between them.

They stand hand in hand in the sunlit room by the window, and Margaret tells him in a trembling voice that she loves him. She has loved him, she thinks, since the day of the riot, though she was too proud to know it. He kisses her gently, as though she were made of glass, and for a long moment neither of them can say a single word.

Aunt Shaw claps her hands with delight when she hears the news, declaring that she has always been fond of the north, and she begins at once to plan a party. Henry Lennox, who has been invited to dine, bows to Margaret with a smile that is only slightly rueful. He wishes her every happiness, behaving in every way exactly as a true friend should.

The mill reopens in the early spring, with its great windows lit and its chimneys smoking once more, and Higgins returns to his place beside Mr Thornton as foreman of the weaving floor. Masters and workers begin, slowly and awkwardly, to talk to each other as men. They talk over the plain meals in the mill kitchen and across the old, hard divisions of the town, and little by little the divisions begin to soften.

Margaret and John Thornton are married in a small church on a bright spring morning, with Dixon, Higgins and Mrs Thornton among the guests. In their home in Milton the north and the south, the stern and the gentle, are joined at last. The story ends on a note of hope that people of different worlds can, with patience and honesty, learn to understand one another.
